sens: Capital city of the Persian kings
Winter residence of the Persian royal court
Center of Persian political power
Setting for the events in the book of Esther
H7800.detail:
1. Susa is a major city in the Middle East, the capital of the Persian kingdom where the kings and their court reside. It is where Nehemiah is serving when he learns of the troubles in Jerusalem (Nehemiah 1:1), and it is from Susa that royal edicts are issued.

2. The city is famous as the winter seat of the king's court, where the splendor and intrigues of Persian royalty take place. It is in Susa that King Ahasuerus holds his royal feast and where Esther enters the king's harem to find favor (Esther 2:3).

3. Susa is the center of political power from which royal decisions radiate throughout the empire, with couriers departing with the king's edicts (Esther 3:15, 8:14).

4. In the book of Esther, Susa becomes the stage for the deliverance of the Jews: it is where Haman prepares his deadly plot, where Queen Esther intercedes for her people, and where the salvation of the Jews is accomplished (Esther 9:11-15).
H7800.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew שׁוּשַׁן (shushan), which literally means "lily" (flower) in Hebrew. This name may evoke the beauty or vegetation of this fertile region of Mesopotamia. Historically, Susa was an ancient city of the Persian Achaemenid Empire, located in Elam on the banks of the Ulai River (or Choaspes). It is one of the great capitals of the ancient world known for its architectural and administrative splendor.
H7800.emploi: Susa appears 19 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the book of Esther (almost all chapters) and a few times in Nehemiah and Daniel. In Esther, it is the main setting for the entire story: it is where Ahasuerus resides, where young women are gathered to be presented to the king (Esther 2:3), where Persian edicts are proclaimed (Esther 3:15, 8:14), and where the massacres and deliverance occur (Esther 9:6-18). In Nehemiah, Nehemiah resides there as the king's official. In Daniel, the prophet has a vision near Susa (Daniel 8:2). The city remains the site of Persian political power and the unfolding of decisive events.
H7800.portee: Susa reminds the reader that even in the lands of exile, far from Jerusalem, God watches over His people. The story of Esther, entirely centered on Susa, shows how God acts through seemingly ordinary human circumstances to save His own. This narrative invites the believer in exile to recognize the hidden presence of God in the places where they find themselves, even far from the promised land.

sens: The inhabitants of Susa, the royal capital of the Persian Empire
H7801.detail: 1. Dehah refers to the people originating from Susa (or Shushan in Hebrew), the great city that was long the administrative heart of the Persian Empire. The word appears in Ezra 4:9, where it lists the peoples and provinces of the Persian Empire that oppose the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem after the exile: Susa is mentioned among the cities whose inhabitants contribute to this letter of protest.
H7801.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the name of the city of Susa (שׁוּשַׁן, Shushan), which means "lily" or "fleur-de-lis" in Persian. This city, located in Mesopotamia (modern Khuzestan in Iran), was one of the royal residences of the Persian kings, notably Ahasuerus. The Hebrew suffix transforms the name of the city into a demonym, that is, a word designating the inhabitants or natives of that place.
H7801.emploi: Dehah appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 4:9. This verse is part of an official correspondence between administrators of various provinces of the Persian Empire and the king, regarding the obstacles to the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem. Susa was a major capital of Persia: it is where Ahasuerus holds his court in the book of Esther, and it is in this geopolitical context that the people of Judah attempt to rebuild their temple.

sens: Son of Ephraim and ancestor of families in the tribe of Ephraim
H7803G.detail: Shuthelah is a man of the tribe of Ephraim, son of Ephraim and brother of Beker, Tahan, Ezer, and Beriah. He gave his name to a family, the Shuthelahites, which was one of the divisions of the tribe of Ephraim at the time of the census in the wilderness. His sons, Eran and Bered, became leaders of families within the people of Israel (Numbers 26:35-36; 1 Chronicles 7:20).
H7803G.origine: The name literally means "noise of breaking" or "noise of crashing." It comes from the Hebrew root evoking a loud sound, a rupture. Shuthelah holds an important place in the genealogy of Ephraim, one of the twelve tribes of Israel: he is the ancestor of the clan of Shuthelahites, from whom major figures like Joshua descend.
H7803G.emploi: Shuthelah is mentioned three times in the Bible, all in genealogical contexts. He first appears in the census of Israel in the wilderness (Numbers 26:35), where his family is listed among the divisions of the tribe of Ephraim. The following verse (Numbers 26:36) details his descendants, particularly Eran, the founder of the family of the Eranites. Another parallel genealogy is found in 1 Chronicles 7:20, which traces the lineage of Ephraim through Shuthelah and his descendants. These passages highlight his foundational role in the genealogical and administrative structure of the tribe.

sens: Man of the tribe of Ephraim during the divided monarchy
H7803H.detail: Shuthelah is a descendant of Ephraim, son of Zabad, mentioned in the genealogy of the tribe of Ephraim. He appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:21, where he is listed among the ancestors of Ephraim. His name literally means "noise of breaking" or "noise of fracture," evoking violence or destruction. Although little known and rarely mentioned in the Scriptures, he is part of the genealogical lineage that traces back to Joshua.
H7803H.origine: The name Shuthelah means "noise of breaking" or "noise of fracture," composed of Hebrew roots evoking a violent sound or destruction. It is formed from a root related to noise or crashing, suggesting an image of strength or power. The name carries a warrior or violent nuance, a common trait in Hebrew names of the time.
H7803H.emploi: Shuthelah is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:21. He appears in the genealogy of Ephraim, presented as the son of Zabad and the father of Ezer and Elead. This genealogical passage establishes his place in the succession of generations of the tribe of Ephraim, although few details are given about his personal life or actions.

sens: To rescue someone from immediate danger, to save them from a deadly situation
To remove someone from the power or authority of an oppressor
To intervene to help someone who trusts
H7804.detail:
1. To deliver means to pull someone from urgent peril, to rescue them from death. When King Nebuchadnezzar threatens the three young Hebrews with the fiery furnace, he ironically asks, "What god will deliver you from my hand?" (Daniel 3:15). The word depicts the act of saving at a critical moment.
2. It also means to remove someone from the grip of an oppressor or tyrannical authority. The three companions of Daniel proclaim, "Our God is able to deliver us from the fiery furnace, and He will deliver us from your hand, O king" (Daniel 3:17) — they fear not only the fire but especially the king who commands it.
3. More broadly, it is to intervene to help someone who places their trust. God "has delivered His servants who trusted in Him" (Daniel 3:28), and the king hopes that the God of Daniel can "deliver" him from the lion's den (Daniel 6:20) — the word implies a relationship of trust between the one who saves and the one who is saved.
H7804.origine: It is an Aramaic verb (the language spoken in Babylon). It comes from the same root as the Hebrew verb shûv (שׁוּב), which means "to return" or "to come back": it conveys the idea of bringing someone back to safety, of restoring them to life. This is why to deliver and to return share the same imagery: bringing back to oneself the one you love.
H7804.emploi: This verb appears only seven times in the Bible, all in the book of Daniel, chapters 3 and 6 — two stories of deadly danger and divine intervention. In Daniel 3, the three young Hebrews confess that God can "deliver" them from the furnace, and then Nebuchadnezzar acknowledges after the events that God has "delivered" them. In Daniel 6, King Darius asks four times whether the God of Daniel can "deliver" him from the lion's den. The verb is always used in the face of extreme threat: fire, wild beast, the hand of an all-powerful king. It is a word for moments of crisis where only God can intervene.
H7804.portee: These verses show that divine deliverance does not depend on earthly power, even royal. It rewards faithfulness — the three young Hebrews "violated the king's order" to remain faithful to God (Daniel 3:28), and that is what saved them. For the Christian, this word reminds us that true security does not come from pleasing the powerful, but from trusting God when we have chosen to obey Him.

sens: To catch sight of, to see something or someone
To direct one's visual attention to a place or a person
To be exposed to view, to be visible
To be affected or marked by something external
H7805.detail:
1. The verb primarily describes the action of seeing, of looking at something or someone — to catch sight of, to fix one's eyes on someone. In Job 20:9, the text states that the eye that looked at the wicked will not look at him again: this conveys the idea of directing visual attention to someone.
2. The word can also mean "to perceive a place" or "to be informed" — to see and recognize a location. In Job 28:7, the bird of prey does not know the path of wisdom, and the eye of the vulture has not perceived it: the animal cannot see or cannot reach that hidden path.
3. By extension, the verb can express the idea that something or someone is seen, exposed to the view of others, or noticed. It is to be visible, to be perceived by others.
4. In Song of Solomon 1:6, where the young girl says, "Do not take notice of my dark complexion," the word also evokes the idea of being marked or altered by an external action (here, the sun that has burned her). To look at or to see is also to notice a visible mark left on someone.
H7805.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׁזַף (shaph) is related to the action of seeing or looking. Its root expresses the idea of directing the gaze toward something, of being aware of it through sight. The word belongs to the family of visual perception verbs in Hebrew, alongside verbs like "to see" (ראה) or "to look" (חָזָה). The basic image is that of the eye turning toward something and becoming aware of it.
H7805.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, all usages provided. In Job 20:9, it describes the gaze directed at the wicked who will disappear. In Job 28:7, it expresses the fact that the eye of the vulture does not perceive the hidden path of wisdom. In Song of Solomon 1:6, it is used in the sense of "to notice" or "to see" the sunburned complexion. The word remains infrequent, and its usages revolve around the idea of seeing, perceiving, or being seen, sometimes with a nuance of noticing a mark or visible change.
H7805.portee: This verb reminds us that nothing escapes the gaze — neither of men nor of God. In Job, it emphasizes that the wicked disappears and that the mysteries of wisdom remain hidden from human eyes. For the believer, this invites reflection on what our eyes can and cannot see, and on the limits of our knowledge in the face of God's plans.

sens: Thread or fabric obtained by twisting together several strands
Made of twisted and interwoven threads
Of fine and regular quality, suitable for linen fabrics intended for the sanctuary
H7806.detail:
1. The word twisted primarily refers to a thread or fabric created by twisting together several strands of linen or another material: it is the action of twisting that gives the thread its strength and smooth appearance. Exodus 26:1 describes the tabernacle "of ten curtains of fine twisted linen."
2. The term then qualifies the result of this twisting: a fabric whose threads are tightly interwoven and present a regular and shiny surface. This technique makes the fabric more durable and beautiful, hence its frequent use for the sacred hangings of the sanctuary (Exodus 27:9: "fine twisted linen curtains, a hundred cubits long").
3. By extension, twisted characterizes the fineness and quality of the fabrics reserved for divine worship: these twisted fabrics, often dyed blue, purple, or scarlet, adorn the courtyard, the ephod, and the veil of the tabernacle, marking the splendor of the place of divine presence (Exodus 39:2: "They made the ephod of gold, of blue, purple, and scarlet thread, and of fine twisted linen").
H7806.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׁזַר (shazar) literally means "to twist" or "to interlace." The word twisted, in French, comes from the Latin "retortus" (twisted again), which exactly conveys this idea of twisted and interwoven threads. The Hebrew verb expresses the action of twisting that transforms simple strands into a solid and uniform thread, an essential action in the making of fine fabrics for the sanctuary.
H7806.emploi: The word twisted appears 21 times in the Old Testament, exclusively in chapters 26 to 39 of Exodus, which detail the construction of the tabernacle and the making of the priestly garments. It always qualifies the fine linen used for the curtains and hangings of the tabernacle (Exodus 26:1, 36:8), for the courtyard (Exodus 27:9, 38:9), for the ephod and breastplate of the high priest (Exodus 28:6, 39:2), and for other elements of worship. The twisted fabric is regularly associated with precious dyes — blue, purple, scarlet — that distinguish the sacred textiles. Its use is therefore highly specialized: it marks the superior quality and holiness of the objects destined for divine service.
H7806.portee: For the Christian reader, the twisted fabric embodies the beauty and care that God requires for what concerns Him: the tabernacle, dwelling of His presence, is not built hastily, but with fine linen, carefully crafted and beautifully colored. This detail reminds us that access to God was not trivial, and that it required preparation, purity, and attention. For those who believe in Jesus, this luxury of ancient worship speaks of the honor given to God and the reverence that should characterize our approach to the Lord.

sens: action of rising up, getting back up after a fall or a lowering
restoration of dignity or honor after humiliation
divine intervention that lifts up one who has bowed down
H7807.detail: 1. The word primarily evokes physical restoration: rising from a low or lowered position. In Job 22:29, when Eliphaz speaks of "restoration," he refers to the moment when one who has experienced humiliation rises up and asks God for help. 2. More broadly, it is the restoration of dignity and honor: the moral and social uplift of one who has been brought low. 3. The spiritual meaning emerges when we understand that this restoration comes from God, who lifts up the one whose gaze has been lowered to the ground due to shame or distress.
H7807.origine: The Hebrew word שַׁח (shach) is related to the idea of being low, downcast, or prostrated. It belongs to the family of words describing states of humility or deprivation: one who is low naturally seeks to rise up. The basic image is that of posture: the head bowed or the body lowered by affliction finds its opposite in restoration.
H7807.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 22:29. In this passage from Eliphaz's speech to Job, the word is placed in a context of consolation and divine promise: after humiliation comes restoration if one turns to God. Eliphaz asserts that anyone who is humiliated and then rises up through prayer benefits from divine protection. It is a rare word, but strategically placed in an affirmation of theodicy: God lifts up the humble.
H7807.portee: For the reader, this verse teaches that humiliation is not final. It can become the path to restoration: by acknowledging our lowliness and need, we call upon God, who lifts us up and looks upon us. It is a word of comfort for those going through trial and shame: divine restoration responds to sincere prostration.

sens: What forms in the mind: an idea, a reflection, a plan
What someone meditates or secretly intends
The hidden intention of the heart
H7808.detail:
1. This word designates the content of the mind — what occupies reflection and forms in thought. In Amos 4:13, God "makes known to man his thoughts": he reveals what man meditates internally, his plans, his most secret intentions. It is thus a living, active thought, carrying intention.
2. The word often emphasizes the hidden or reserved nature of what is thought: it is not what one says aloud, but what remains in the intimacy of the heart. Only God can truly know these thoughts and bring them to light.
3. By extension, it designates the intentions or plans that someone harbors: what one intends to do, what one secretly schemes. It is particularly useful for speaking of the thoughts that God reveals or critiques.
H7808.origine: This original Hebrew root evokes the idea of deep meditation, of reflection that develops. The word belongs to the family of terms that describe the activity of the mind and heart — this inner world where plans and intentions are formed. In biblical context, thought is never purely intellectual: it is always linked to moral intention, to what one intends to do.
H7808.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Amos 4:13. In this prophetic context, God is the one who "knows the thoughts" of man — it is one of his divine prerogatives. The rarity of the word does not diminish its importance: on the contrary, this unique usage places it in a major declaration about God's omniscience. It is a God who scrutinizes the inner self, who is not deceived by appearances, who sees even the most secret thoughts.
H7808.portee: For the believer, this passage reminds us that nothing escapes God — not even our most hidden thoughts. This can initially be frightening: how could I hide from God? But it is also an invitation to honesty before him and to purify our thoughts. God knows us completely, not to condemn us blindly, but to transform us from within.

sens: To give something to someone to please or influence them
To offer gifts for a self-interested or corrupt purpose
To buy someone's favor with gifts
H7809.detail:
1. The word designates the action of giving a gift to someone. In Job 6:22, the suffering man asks his friends: "Did I say to you, 'Give me something, make gifts for me'?" meaning: "Did I ever ask you for any gift?" The verb here evokes the simple act of offering a present.
2. The word takes on a negative connotation when the gift aims to corrupt or buy favor. In Ezekiel 16:33, unfaithful Jerusalem "has given gifts to all your lovers," seeking through these presents to attract them and ensure their loyalty — it is a self-interested exchange. The gift then becomes a means of seduction or corruption, like one offered to a magistrate to obtain a favorable sentence.
H7809.origine: The Hebrew verb shabat literally means "to give" or "to present." It is related to the idea of handing something over to someone to satisfy them or gain their goodwill. The family of the word includes the noun shabat (gift, present, bribe), which can refer to both a generous gift and a corrupt bribe depending on the context. The word expresses the fundamental exchange: to offer in order to receive.
H7809.emploi: The verb shabat appears only twice in the preserved Hebrew Bible. In these two usages, it describes the action of presenting gifts, but the context guides the meaning. In Job 6:22, it is a rhetorical question from the suffering man denying having asked for alms — the gift is innocent there. In Ezekiel 16:33, applied to the prostituted Jerusalem, the word acquires a connotation of corruption: she buys her lovers with gifts. The fundamental meaning remains "to give a gift," but the Bible uses it to describe both generosity and carnal seduction or corruption.
H7809.portee: This word reminds us that generosity can become an instrument of manipulation or corruption. For the believer, it invites us to examine our intentions when we give: is it pure liberality, or an attempt to buy favor or affection? The Bible warns against using gifts as weapons of seduction or corruption, especially when, as in the case of Jerusalem, it reflects unfaithfulness to God.

sens: A benefit, money, or a valuable object offered to someone to gain their favor or influence their decision
A gift given secretly or with a hidden intention to corrupt
A gift that blinds the judgment of the recipient and leads them to act against justice
H7810.detail: 1. The שֹׁחַד (shohad) primarily refers to a present or material gift — money, gold, a precious object — offered to someone with the aim of corrupting them or gaining their favor. Ahaz sends gold and silver as a "present" to the king of Assyria (2 Kings 16:8), which in this context resembles a forced tribute, but the word often includes the idea of seduction or manipulation. 2. The term mainly describes the bribe slipped to a judge, leader, or official to make them turn a blind eye or change their verdict. Exodus 23:8 explicitly forbids it: "You shall not accept a bribe, for a bribe blinds the clear-sighted and subverts the cause of the just." It is the image of wealth that disturbs moral vision, clouding discernment. 3. Proverbs 17:8 refers to this present as "a precious stone in the eyes of the one who receives it" — a treasure for the one who covets it — and notes its formidable effectiveness: "Wherever they turn, they succeed." The bribe works; that is why it is so dangerous and condemned by the Law.
H7810.origine: The word שֹׁחַד (shohad) comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of "breaking," "bending," or "diverting." Its exact etymology remains debated, but its meaning reveals a profound image: the bribe is what "breaks" righteousness, what "bends" justice. The Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) often translates it as δῶρον (dôron, "gift") or δωροδοκία (dôrodokia, "acceptance of gifts"), terms that emphasize the self-serving and corrupting nature of the present.
H7810.emploi: The word שֹׁחַד appears 21 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of Law and Wisdom. The Law categorically forbids it: Exodus 23:8 commands the judge not to accept it, Deuteronomy 10:17 and 16:19 remind that God shows no partiality and does not accept bribes, and Deuteronomy 27:25 curses anyone who accepts a present to condemn the innocent. Proverbs studies it as a formidable reality: it "succeeds" (17:8), it can "appease anger" (21:14), and corrupt leaders love and seek it (Isaiah 1:23, 5:23, Micah 3:11). Job 15:34 and other passages show that those who accept bribes plunge into ruin. The word always denotes moral corruption, never a simple gift of friendship.
H7810.portee: This word teaches the reader that justice has no price and that anyone who governs, judges, or must act impartially must refuse all corruption, no matter how enticing it may be. It also reminds how the bribe "blinds" — it obscures moral judgment and makes one forget the fear of God. For the modern believer, it serves as a warning against any form of self-serving compromise, any dubious transaction that claims to "make things right": God sees, and He curses these practices.

sens: To move in water by using the limbs
To be immersed, bathed in liquid
To exhaust oneself through repeated movements
H7811.detail: 1. To swim means to move in water by waving the arms and legs: it is the image of the swimmer extending their hands to move forward (Isaiah 25:11). 2. The word also evokes the idea of being plunged, submerged in a liquid: the psalmist whose bed "is bathed" and "soaked" with tears expresses this submersion (Psalms 6:7). 3. By extension, to swim means to exhaust oneself through repeated and intense efforts, as one tires from crying or making movements in water: this is why "strength" conveys this meaning in Psalms 6:7, where the verb expresses the exhaustion of a body tortured by grief.
H7811.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׂחָה comes from a root that depicts the undulating movement of one who moves in water. The fundamental meaning is physical and concrete: to swim. The biblical language extends this gesture beyond water: it applies to any submersion or immersion, even metaphorical, and to the exhaustion caused by repeated movements of the body.
H7811.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Bible in Hebrew. In Isaiah 25:11, the swimmer extends their hands in the water — it is the image of the swimming motion. In Psalms 6:7, the same verb describes the psalmist submerged by his tears: he exhausts himself, his limbs flailing under the weight of pain, like someone swimming in tears. The context changes the apparent meaning: from a physical and voluntary action (to swim) to a passive and involuntary suffering (to be plunged, to exhaust oneself).
H7811.portee: For the believer reading Psalms 6:7, this verb gives substance to suffering: it is not a mere abstract sorrow, but a total submersion of the body, a physical exhaustion due to mourning. In Isaiah 25:11, the swimmer who stretches out their hands to save themselves becomes the image of human pride that struggles in vain against God. These two images remind us that the suffering of the heart affects the whole being, and that any resistance to God is as futile as trying to save oneself by swimming.

sens: To incline the body and forehead to the ground as a sign of respect or submission
To show devotion or obedience to an authority
To render worship to God or a deity
To express adoration or prayer
H7812.detail:
1. To bow down is primarily a bodily gesture: one bends, inclines deeply, and may even touch the ground with their forehead (Genesis 18:2: Abraham runs to meet three visitors "and bowed down to the ground"). It is the supreme gesture of humility and respect towards someone greater.
2. This posture expresses submission and allegiance: one bows down before a king or superior to acknowledge their authority and seek their favor (1 Kings 2:19: when King Solomon bows down before his mother Bathsheba, he honors her prominent place).
3. To bow down before God or an idol is the act of worship par excellence: it is to recognize divinity, to pay homage, to submit entirely to it (Exodus 24:1: Moses and the elders go up to bow down before the Lord).
4. The gesture can also express prayer, adoration, the request for grace: by bowing down, one places themselves in the attitude of one who pleads and awaits a response from the one before whom they kneel.
H7812.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁחָה (sha.chah) comes from a root that evokes the idea of bending, inclining. The physical gesture is at the heart of the meaning: it is the body that speaks before words. In the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament), it is often rendered by words that also mean "to bow down" or "to kneel." This gesture was universal in antiquity to show respect and subordination.
H7812.emploi: The verb to bow down is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible (166 occurrences recorded). It appears everywhere: in Genesis (Abraham, Jacob, and his sons bow down), in Exodus and Leviticus (acts of worship and adoration), in the historical books (respect towards kings and authorities). It denotes both the worship rendered to the true God (Exodus 34:8: bowing down in the presence of the Lord) and that, condemned, rendered to idols (Isaiah 2:8: the Israelites bow down before the idols they have made). The gesture can be a private act of prayer or a public act of religious ceremony. Gradually, the word can also simply evoke the inclination of respect in everyday life.
H7812.portee: For the believer, this word reminds what the proper posture before God is: that of humility, recognition, and total dependence. To bow down is to abandon one's pride and acknowledge that God alone is worthy of worship. It also teaches that respect for legitimate authorities (parents, kings, elders) reflects the respect due to God. But the Bible also warns: to bow down before idols or creatures instead of God alone is great unfaithfulness.

sens: To move in water by using the body
To travel on the surface or in the depths of a body of water
Figuratively: to be overwhelmed, to face the impossible
H7813.detail:
1. To swim means to move in water using one's own strength, coordinating arms and legs. It is the act of crossing or progressing through water. In Ezekiel 47:5, the prophet sees a river so deep that one would need to swim to cross it: the water is no longer shallow, it covers the head.
2. The word also denotes the state of one who is submerged by water, who must swim to survive or advance. It conveys the idea of sinking into a depth that requires all one's efforts.
3. By spiritual extension, swimming figuratively represents facing a trial that exceeds our natural strength, like water that continually rises. The prophet Ezekiel expresses through this word the human impossibility in the face of the power of this river of life that God causes to spring forth.
H7813.origine: The Hebrew word שׂחוּ (sachu) comes from a root that evokes the movement of gliding and floating in water. It is rarely used in biblical Hebrew. Its image is that of a body being carried and propelled by water, in contrast to walking on dry land. It is a concrete term that refers to a natural and observable physical act.
H7813.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 47:5. It is in a prophetic vision where Ezekiel sees a miraculous river flowing from the temple. As he moves into its waters, they become so deep that he can no longer cross them on foot: he would need to swim. This context is one of water that grows, elevates, and soon exceeds all human measure. The prophet uses this verb to mark the point where a person must give up their ordinary approach and accept being carried by something that surpasses them.
H7813.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize the limits of their own strength. In the face of God's works, there comes a moment when one can no longer advance by their own efforts: one must be lifted, carried by what surpasses them. It is an image of surrendering to divine grace, of trusting in what supports us when we can no longer hold on. For the believer, it is a call to accept that God works beyond what we can control.

sens: Expression of joy and gladness through laughter
Hollow laughter, lacking depth or true contentment
Mockery, derision, ridicule directed at someone
Amusement, entertainment, play
H7814.detail:
1. Joyful laughter is the natural expression of the joy and gladness of the heart. It is the laughter that arises spontaneously when one experiences happiness or relief. Job speaks of a mouth filled with "shouts" of joy, and Psalm 126 describes the laughter of the freed who have seen the Lord accomplish great things.
2. However, laughter can also be hollow and deceptive: a surface laughter behind which distress hides. Ecclesiastes observes that "even in laughter, the heart may be in anguish," showing that laughter is not a guarantee of true happiness.
3. Laughter becomes mockery when it turns against someone to ridicule them. Moab becomes "an object of derision," and Jeremiah complains of being the mockery of everyone: his prophetic message makes him ridiculous in the eyes of those who listen to him.
4. Finally, laughter can simply refer to amusement or entertainment, as in Ecclesiastes 10:19 where meals are made "for enjoyment": it is the play and amusement of leisure.
H7814.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that conveys the idea of laughter and lightness. It is used for both sincere laughter and mockery: the same act of laughter can express joy or disdain, depending on the heart of the one laughing. This ambiguity is very alive in the Bible, where laughter reveals the true heart.
H7814.emploi: This word appears fourteen times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the wisdom books (Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes) and in the prophets (Jeremiah, Lamentations). Job and the Psalms use laughter to express restored joy and gladness. But Ecclesiastes constantly contrasts it with the sorrow and distress of the heart: the wise see that laughter alone is not wisdom. The prophets Jeremiah and Lamentations use it for the bitter mockery directed against Israel or its enemies. The context thus changes the meaning: laughter is joyful among the freed, ambiguous in Ecclesiastes, cruel among the mockers.
H7814.portee: Biblical laughter teaches us that true joy comes from the Lord and His works (as in Psalm 126), but that laughter alone cannot fill the afflicted heart. The Bible warns us against mocking laughter that hurts and belittles others: it invites us instead to deep joy, not superficial mockery. Finally, the mockery of God's enemies is fleeting: only joy in God is lasting.

sens: Black color, absence of light
Darkening of the skin, dark or livid complexion
Figurative darkness, the gloom of affliction
H7815.detail: 1. Darkness is primarily the color black itself, the absence or total absorption of light. It is the darkest shade one can see. 2. In the context of Lamentations 4:8, darkness describes the complexion of the inhabitants of Jerusalem reduced to famine: their skin has become black, dried up, clinging to their bones, so much so that suffering has transformed them physically. The image evokes a nearly monstrous distortion of the human face due to deprivation. 3. Figuratively, darkness can evoke moral or spiritual obscurity, the gloom of distress and judgment, although this meaning is implicit rather than explicit in biblical texts.
H7815.origine: The Hebrew word שְׁחוֹר (shéhor) comes from a simple and ancient root denoting the color black. It is an adjective that has sometimes been substantivized to denote darkness itself, that is, the state of being black. The word belongs to the basic vocabulary of color in Hebrew, alongside white and red.
H7815.emploi: This word appears very rarely in the Bible (only once in the attested uses). It is found in Lamentations 4:8, in one of the most poignant passages of Scripture: the description of the survivors of besieged Jerusalem, whose physical appearance has been transformed by famine to the point that they can no longer be recognized. The darkness of the complexion here is a symptom of the disaster and curse that have struck the city. The context is not aesthetic or descriptive, but dramatic and theological: the darkness of the human face embodies the horror of destruction.
H7815.portee: This word reminds us that in the Bible, the physical and visible description of suffering reflects a spiritual reality. The sight of these men with faces darkened by famine is not a mere humanitarian tragedy: it is the fruit of God's judgment on the sin and unbelief of Jerusalem. It invites us to recognize that material desolation often externalizes an inner distance from the Lord.

sens: excavation dug in the ground to fall into
trap or pitfall caused by one's own malice
punishment that the wicked brings upon themselves
H7816.detail:
1. A pit is a hole dug in the ground, deep enough for someone to fall in and get hurt. It is the concrete image of the word: a dangerous cavity where one tumbles down (Proverbs 28:10).
2. The pit becomes a trap: the one who digs it risks falling into it themselves. This conveys the idea that malice turns back against its author, just as the wicked who leads others astray ultimately ends up lost themselves.
3. Figuratively, the pit represents the punishment, destruction, or ruin that the wicked bring upon themselves through their own wickedness. It symbolizes the fatal consequences of their actions.
H7816.origine: The Hebrew word שְׁחוּת (shékhout) likely comes from a root related to the idea of digging, of making a hole. It is a concrete word that first describes a physical excavation, then is used figuratively to denote the traps and ruins that people cause for themselves through their conduct.
H7816.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Proverbs 28:10. In this verse, the wise man teaches that the one who leads the upright into evil "falls into the pit he has dug." The pit here is both the material trap and the symbol of the fate that the wicked brings upon themselves: their malice turns against them. The contrast with the "upright who inherit happiness" shows that the pit is reserved for those who act wickedly.
H7816.portee: This verse reminds the believer that divine justice is certain: evil never goes unpunished, and the one who sets a trap for others will fall into it themselves. It is an exhortation to righteousness: do not seek to harm your neighbor, for this intention will turn into personal ruin. The pit also teaches that our destiny is not predetermined by chance, but shaped by our actions.

sens: To bend the body forward, to stoop, to kneel
To be crushed, overwhelmed, rendered powerless
To be humiliated, lowered in pride or honor
To wither, to faint, to lose courage
To bend in pain, grief, or mourning
H7817.detail:
1. To bow down is to bend one's body forward to greet, honor, or adorn someone greater. It is the gesture of respect and submission. Thus in Job 9:13, "the supports of pride bow down before Him," meaning that even the proudest forces bend before God's power.
2. To be crushed means to be overwhelmed, rendered incapable of resisting. It is the effect of a superior force bending you down. In Isaiah 2:9, "the small will be crushed" describes not only a low position but a state of total weakness.
3. To be humiliated means to lose one's honor and elevation, to be publicly lowered. It is especially pride that is crushed: in Isaiah 5:15, "the great will be humbled" means that those who thought themselves strong and important will see their pride broken.
4. To wither or faint means to lose strength, to weaken morally and physically. In Psalms 42:7, "my soul is cast down within me" expresses inner collapse, when the spirit has no more resilience.
5. To bend in pain or mourning means to express grief through a low and bent posture. In Psalms 35:14, the psalmist says, "I bowed down in sadness" thinking of one who suffers: the body mimics the weight of the heart.
H7817.origine: The Hebrew verb "shachach" primarily expresses the physical action of bending, bowing down. The starting image is that of the body bending under a weight, whether respectful (bowing the head before someone) or destructive (being crushed by a force). The word can also mean to lower oneself in prostration or to be brought to nothing. The root carries the idea of an inferior position, whether physical or moral.
H7817.emploi: This verb appears 21 times in the Bible, mainly in the Psalms and in the prophet Isaiah. It first describes the religious or social gesture: bowing down before God or a king, as a sign of respect (Job 9:13). But it often depicts the action of oppression: being crushed by misfortune, the enemy, or God's judgment. The Psalms use it to express inner distress: the soul crushed by grief or trials (Psalms 42:7). Isaiah uses it in announcements of divine judgment, when the pride of men will be humbled and brought low (Isaiah 5:15). The word always carries a nuance of weakness, submission, or suffering — it is never neutral.
H7817.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the Christian about two essential truths. First, that true greatness consists in humbly bowing before God, not out of servile fear, but out of respectful reverence (Proverbs 14:19 suggests that humility leads to good). Second, that our oppressors and our proud pretensions will be crushed by God's just judgment. For the one who suffers, this verb also validates their pain: the crushed soul, the body bent in mourning, is a language that God hears and recognizes.

sens: To exert pressure on something to extract juice or content
To crush or compress between the hands or under a force
H7818.detail:
1. To press means to strongly push on something to extract a liquid: it is the action of squeezing juice from grapes by pressing them in the hands or against a surface. This is exactly what Pharaoh's cupbearer does in Genesis 40:11: he takes the grapes and presses them into the cup to obtain wine.
2. More broadly, the word describes any action of compressing or crushing something by exerting force, as one would press a fruit or substance between the fingers.
H7818.origine: The verb הקח (sa.chat) comes from a root that evokes the idea of squeezing, compressing. The starting image is that of the hand gripping or crushing to extract. In Hebrew, this verb belongs to the family of words that describe physical actions of transformation: pressing grapes means transforming them into juice.
H7818.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 40:11, in the context of the cupbearer's dream. The cupbearer tells Joseph how, in his dream, he held Pharaoh's cup, took grapes, and pressed them to make wine. It is a concrete and precise verb, used to describe a daily and domestic action: the ordinary work of one who prepares wine from fresh grapes.
H7818.portee: This word reminds us of the simple and useful tasks of ordinary life. In its context, it highlights how the cupbearer was a trusted servant, accustomed to preparing Pharaoh's drinks: it is a detail that shows the responsibility and honor of his position before his fall into prison.

sens: To cut the throat or kill an animal intended for food
To kill an animal as a sacrifice to God
To kill a person, especially in human sacrifice or execution
To strike or shape an object (such as coins)
H7819A.detail:
1. Slaughter primarily means to cut the throat of an animal to kill it for the purpose of eating. This is the most common meaning: animals are prepared for meals, as when Abraham reaches out to slaughter his son Isaac whom he believes he must offer to God (Genesis 22:10).

2. The word also applies to religious sacrifice: a ram, bull, or lamb is slaughtered not for eating, but to offer to God, fulfilling the Law. The priests slaughter the offerings in front of the tent of meeting and sprinkle the blood on the altar, as seen in the sacrifices of Leviticus 3:8 and Leviticus 16:11.

3. Slaughter can also refer to the murder of a person, particularly in cases of human sacrifice or bloody executions. Isaiah denounces those who slaughter children in the valleys (Isaiah 57:5), and the text recounts how the king's sons were slaughtered (2 Kings 10:7).

4. In a rare and figurative sense, the word can describe the shaping of an object by striking, such as coins being hammered or shaped.
H7819A.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁחַט (shaḥat) comes from a root that evokes the idea of cutting or slicing. It belongs to the same family as other words denoting violence or death. The image is very concrete: that of the blade cutting the throat. The context of sacrifice in the Bible shows that this act is not considered brutal or immoral, but as an act ordained by God, laden with religious significance.
H7819A.emploi: The verb "slaughter" appears 69 times in the Old Testament, particularly in Leviticus and the books of Exodus and Kings. It is almost always related to sacrifices: the priests slaughter the sin offerings, guilt offerings, and peace offerings. It is also found during Passover, where Moses commands the people to slaughter the lamb (Exodus 12:6, 12:21). The word also denotes murder: when the murderers of the king slaughter his sons (2 Kings 10:7), or when Jeremiah is thrown into prison by Zedekiah after the princes denounce him for speaking against violence. The text thus shows the tension between the sacrifice ordained by God and murder, both expressed by the same verb.
H7819A.portee: This word reminds the reader that biblical worship is not a vague or spiritual matter: it engages the body, blood, and life itself. The slaughtering of the sacrificed animal foreshadows the sacrifice of Christ, whose blood shed on the cross takes away the sins of the world. Understanding this physical reality of sacrifice helps to grasp the depth of what Jesus accomplished for us. It is also a warning against murder and violence: unjustly shed blood cries out for vengeance, while blood shed in obedience to God reconciles.

sens: abandonment of faithfulness to God
moral and religious deviation
guilt in sin
H7819B.detail:
1. The word denotes unfaithfulness, that is, the abandonment of the faithfulness owed to God. In Hosea 5:2, the "unfaithful" are those who turn away from the covenant with the Lord through their corrupt sacrifices and religious practices: they dig their own pit of sin.
2. It is a moral and religious deviation, a betrayal of the trust placed in us. Those who act this way willingly plunge into crime and guilt.
3. The word also carries the idea of guilt and personal responsibility: it is not circumstances that lead to evil, but a conscious choice to distance oneself from God.
H7819B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of turning away, turning one's back. In the Hebrew Bible, it describes the attitude of one who deliberately breaks their commitment to God—not out of weakness, but through an act of active rebellion. The Segond translates it here as "unfaithful" or "unfaithfulness" to express this breach of covenant.
H7819B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Hosea 5:2. The prophet Hosea denounces the Israelites who, far from sincerely seeking God, dig their own ruin through their corrupt sacrifices and criminal acts. It is in the context of Israel's unfaithfulness to the Lord's covenant—moral, religious, and spiritual unfaithfulness—that this word takes on its full force.
H7819B.portee: This word reminds the believer that unfaithfulness to God is never a mere passive failing: it is an active choice that leads one into sin. Hosea warns us that even outward religious practices do not redeem a broken covenant at heart. It is a call to examine our own faithfulness to God.

sens: Struck, shaped by hammering
That has undergone a process of striking or hammering
That is formed by repeated beating
H7820.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of metalworking: striking with a hammer to shape a piece of gold or silver. Beaten gold was an ancient technique for shaping precious metals. This is exactly what King Solomon did: his shields were made of "beaten gold" (1 Kings 10:16), meaning that the gold had been hammered and worked to obtain ornamental plates.
2. More broadly, the word describes anything that has been shaped by repeated blows, through intensive work. It is not raw gold, but transformed gold, refined by labor. The image evokes the patience of the craftsman and the beauty that arises from meticulous work.
H7820.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to strike" or "to beat." It is a verb that describes the physical action of striking: the beating of metals to shape them. It can also refer to the beating of wheat or flax, that is, the work that separates the grain from the chaff. The same root appears in other contexts where striking or beating something is involved.
H7820.emploi: This word appears only four times in the Bible, always in passages concerning King Solomon and his treasures. In 1 Kings 10:16-17 and its parallel in 2 Chronicles 9:15-16, it precisely describes the material of the king's golden shields: "beaten gold." It is a technical description of the work of the goldsmith, emphasizing the quality and care taken in the making of these luxury items. The context shows that this worked gold was part of the wealth and splendor of Solomon's palace.
H7820.portee: This word reminds us that the beauty and richness of the temple and the king's palace reflected the splendor of God. The beaten gold, carefully worked by artisans, symbolized excellence and devotion put to the service of the Lord. It also speaks to the value of well-done work: it is through patient and repeated labor that true beauty is born.

sens: Action d'immoler une victime, de la tuer selon le rite
Mise à mort d'un animal en sacrifice au culte
H7821.detail:
1. Immolation is the act of killing an animal intended for sacrifice. The word refers to the concrete gesture, the ritual slaughter of a victim — lamb, goat, bull — according to the rules established by the Law of Moses. In 2 Chronicles 30:17, the Levites are responsible for immolating the Passover victims for those who were unable to purify themselves: it is an official, priestly act done with religious intention.
2. More broadly, immolation is the bloody offering itself, the act of giving the life of the victim to God. It expresses the consecration of the people and the atonement for their sins.
H7821.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root שׁחט (sha.khat), which means "to slaughter" or "to kill." It is a concrete verb, related to the act of cutting the throat of the victim with a knife. The root is used throughout the vocabulary of biblical sacrifices, particularly in the instructions of Leviticus. This word belongs to the semantic field of Israel's sacrificial worship.
H7821.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible (2 Chronicles 30:17). It refers to the ritual immolation of the Passover victims by the Levites. This unique occurrence shows that the term is technical: it denotes a precise and sacred action, reserved for the context of worship, different from the simple slaughter of an animal for food. The usage in 2 Chronicles emphasizes the role of the priests and Levites in the faithful execution of the sacrifices of the Law.
H7821.portee: Immolation reminds the believer of the cost of sin and the necessity of offering to present oneself before God. It also evokes the death of Jesus Christ, the Lamb slain once for all. Understanding this term helps the Christian grasp the depth of the Old Testament sacrifice and its continuity with the perfect sacrifice of Calvary.

sens: Covered with panels or wood paneling
Interior lining of a wall or structure
H7824.detail:
1. The word refers to a surface covered with wooden panels. It is the image of a wall or partition to which wood has been affixed for protection or decoration. In Ezekiel's vision of the temple, the interior walls of the vestibules and galleries were "covered" with wood in this manner.

2. By extension, it can refer to the paneling or the covering itself — the layer of wood that lines the wall. The passage in Ezekiel 41:16 shows that this wooden covering extended from the floor to the closed windows, thus forming a coherent decoration and protection of the temple's interior space.
H7824.origine: The Hebrew word belongs to a root that evokes the idea of covering or clothing. The initial image is that of a layer applied to a surface for protection or beautification. This type of vocabulary was common in the description of temple constructions, where precious wood played an important role.
H7824.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 41:16, in the detailed description of the prophetic vision of the future temple. Ezekiel precisely enumerates the different parts of the restored temple: the inner sanctuary, the vestibules, the thresholds, the windows, and the galleries. This passage illustrates how, in this vision, the temple walls were covered with wood from the floor to the windows, emphasizing the beauty and holiness of the place.
H7824.portee: This architectural detail reveals the importance that the Bible attributes to the beauty and order of the temple, the place of God's presence. The wooden covering is not a mere superfluous ornament: it reflects the care and majesty with which the temple should be built. For the reader, this invites consideration that the worship rendered to God deserves respect and dignity in every detail.

sens: A hole dug in the ground, a deep excavation
Figuratively: a state of deep distress or mortal danger
Figuratively: a grip of evil or the enemy from which one cannot escape
H7825.detail:
1. In the literal sense, a pit is a hole dug in the ground, often deep and difficult to escape from. In the Bible, it is a place of captivity, imprisonment, or death.

2. Figuratively, the pit represents extreme distress, the affliction that engulfs the sufferer. It is the cry of the sick or oppressed: "He sent His word and healed them, He delivered them from the pit" (Psalms 107:20). The pit here is the image of deadly illness, of despair from which only God's power can deliver us.

3. The pit also refers to the trap or snare of the enemy, the danger from which one is imprisoned. When Lamentations says that the Lord's anointed "has been caught in their pits" (Lamentations 4:20), this word evokes the cruel grip of those who have captured him, a captivity from which there seems to be no escape.
H7825.origine: The Hebrew word shekhit comes from a root that means to dig or make a cavity. It shares its family with words expressing the idea of destruction or ruin. In biblical Hebrew, this term appears rarely: only twice in the preserved texts. It is a concrete word that has naturally taken on figurative meanings to describe all that engulfs and destroys man — illness, captivity, perdition.
H7825.emploi: The word pit appears twice in the provided biblical usages. In the Psalms, in the context of deliverance, it denotes the danger or illness from which God saves His people by His word. In Lamentations, it describes the captivity and war trap into which conquered Jerusalem has fallen. Each time, the pit is what kills or paralyzes, and the mention of God — His word, His power — is the announcement of deliverance. The word remained rare enough to retain its weight: to mention a pit was to speak of certain death, of a situation without human remedy.
H7825.portee: The pit reminds us that the afflictions of the believer — illness, captivity, oppression, sin — are deep realities from which we cannot extricate ourselves alone. But the Bible uses this word to say that God pulls us out: it is a call to cry out to Him in distress, to trust Him even when everything seems hopeless. Recognizing that we are in a pit is to accept our weakness and open ourselves to the Lord's intervention.

sens: The great carnivorous feline, king of beasts
Power and ferocity in imagery
The violent and devastating attack
The imminent threat or insurmountable obstacle
H7826.detail:
1. The lion is the animal itself, the most fearsome of wild beasts in the Middle East. It is a powerful and violent predator: its roar terrifies (Job 4:10), its strength crushes anyone who dares to confront it (Job 10:16).

2. The Bible uses the lion to evoke a destructive power or a terrible authority. God Himself acts "like a lion" against Israel (Hosea 5:14), thus revealing His judgment strength: He tears and carries off His prey, and no one can reclaim what He has seized.

3. The lion also represents a very concrete threat or an immediate danger from which one seeks to escape. The sluggard pretends there is a lion on the road to avoid working (Proverbs 26:13) — a fanciful excuse, for the real lion does not inhabit the streets.

4. For the believer, walking on the lion without fear (Psalms 91:13) symbolizes triumph over every enemy through divine protection: it is the image of spiritual victory over what seemed invincible.
H7826.origine: The Hebrew word שַׁחַל (shachal) designates the lion, this great predator well known in ancient Levant. Its image is one of brute power, ferocity, and mortal danger. It is a stable word in biblical Hebrew, without significant variation in meaning. The root evokes overwhelming strength and the violation of what is closed — the lion forces what resists.
H7826.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated mainly in biblical wisdom (Job, Proverbs, Psalms) and prophecy (Hosea). Job uses it to describe the real threat: the roar of the lion, its relentless pursuit (Job 4:10, 10:16). In Proverbs, it becomes the excuse of the sluggard, showing its status as a proverbial danger (Proverbs 26:13). The Psalter uses it in a promise of victory: the righteous will tread upon the lion without fear (Psalms 91:13). Finally, for the prophets, the lion becomes the face of God: Hosea says that the Lord will act "like a lion" against His unfaithful people, showing that divine power can be terrifying and destructive.
H7826.portee: The lion reveals to the believer that God fears nothing and possesses a power capable of destroying every enemy. But it also teaches that the fear of danger, often exaggerated, can paralyze us: the sluggard invents lions to avoid acting. Finally, the promise of Psalms 91 assures that whoever takes refuge in God walks without fear over powers that seem invincible — an image of the victory of faith.

sens: a fragrant substance used in the incense of the sanctuary
material derived from a marine shellfish
H7827.detail:
1. The fragrant gum is an ingredient in the composition of the sacred incense burned in the tabernacle. In Exodus 30:34, the Lord commands Moses to mix it with stacte, galbanum, and pure frankincense in equal amounts to form the "composed perfume" of the sanctuary. It is an element of worship, intended to create a pleasing aroma to God during sacrifices.
2. Specifically, it is a dried substance obtained from a fragrant gland of the marine shellfish called murex. This whitish substance, once prepared and burned, releases a sweet and lasting aroma, similar to amber or vanilla. Its high price and rarity made it precious in antiquity.
H7827.origine: The Hebrew word שְׁחֵלֶת likely comes from the root שָׁחַל which describes the action of digging or boring, referring to how this material is extracted from the shellfish. The Greek term "onyx" and the Latin "unguis" have retained the memory of the word "gum" because the substance resembles the shape and texture of a scale or a nail. In the Greek version of the Old Testament, this word was well known among Mediterranean peoples as a luxury ingredient.
H7827.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Exodus 30:34, in the precise description of the formula for the sanctuary incense. Moses receives the divine command to prepare this mixture of spices, including the fragrant gum, to perfume the holy place during religious services. This uniqueness shows the ritual importance and sacredness of this substance in Israel's worship: it is not just a perfume, but a material consecrated exclusively for the service of God.
H7827.portee: The fragrant gum reminds us that the worship of the God of Israel engages all the senses: sight, hearing, and also smell. This rare and costly material testifies that God deserves the best gifts. It also invites us to meditate on prayer as a "fragrance that rises to heaven," pleasing to the Lord: our worship should ascend pure and precious before Him.

sens: A sea bird with white and gray plumage
A bird declared unclean by Mosaic Law and forbidden for consumption
H7828.detail:
1. The seagull is an aquatic bird, recognizable by its white and gray plumage, that lives near coasts and lakes. It is a hunter and scavenger that feeds on fish and leftovers.
2. In the list of unclean animals in Leviticus and Deuteronomy, the seagull is among the birds that the Israelites were not to eat. Its status as a carnivorous or scavenging bird made it incompatible with the ritual purity laws of God's people.
H7828.origine: The Hebrew word שַׁחַף (shachaph) designates a sea bird. Its exact etymology remains debated, but it likely refers to a characteristic behavior of this animal — perhaps its cry or its way of diving. The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible.
H7828.emploi: The word "seagull" appears twice in the Old Testament, both in the purity lists of Mosaic Law: in Leviticus 11:16 and Deuteronomy 14:15, in the same context and with the same other birds (ostrich, owl, hawk). These lists aimed to teach the Israelites to distinguish the clean from the unclean by observing creation. The seagull is mentioned simply for its status as a forbidden bird, with no detail about its appearance or habits.
H7828.portee: This mention of the seagull reminds the reader that the holiness of the people of Israel also extended to daily life: what one eats, how one lives. For the Christian, these ancient laws no longer apply (Acts 10), but they invite reflection on what truly nourishes the soul and on moral vigilance in small matters.

sens: A lung disease that progressively weakens
A divine plague sent as punishment for transgressions of the covenant
H7829.detail:
1. Consumption is a lung disease that consumes the body, making it languid and progressively exhausting it. The word suggests a slow destruction of the organism, a kind of wasting of vital forces. It often appears associated with fever in biblical punishments: in Leviticus 26:16, the Lord promises to send consumption and fever upon those who reject Him.
2. Figuratively, consumption becomes a divine punishment, one of the calamities that the Lord sends to His people to bring them back to obedience. It is added to other terrifying plagues: in Deuteronomy 28:22, it appears in a long list of diseases affecting those who transgress the covenant.
H7829.origine: The Hebrew word שַׁחֶפֶת comes from a root that expresses the idea of exhaustion and decay. As a disease, it is linked to the image of a body that weakens and slowly consumes itself, hence the French term "consumption" which comes from the Latin consumere (to consume, to exhaust). It is a concrete physical affliction, but the Bible imbues it with religious significance: it becomes a sign of the rupture of the covenant with God.
H7829.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the blessings and curses of the covenant. In Leviticus 26:16, it is announced as one of the plagues that will strike the disobedient people. In Deuteronomy 28:22, it is among the diseases sent by God upon those who violate the commandments of the Lord. These two passages make it a characteristic divine punishment, closely linked to the violation of the covenant: not a common disease, but a direct intervention from God. It is often paired with fever, suggesting a disease that is both consuming and burning.
H7829.portee: For the believer reading these texts, consumption reminds us that infidelity to God has material and visible consequences: the body itself becomes the theater of the rupture with the covenant. It teaches the seriousness of abandoning God, but also, implicitly, that faithfulness to His commandments is a source of life and health. These ancient verses, far from directly concerning us, invite us to reflect on the link between our relationship with God and our well-being.

sens: A wild animal of noble appearance, majestic and imposing
A haughty, dominating beast that rules by its power
H7830.detail:
1. The word first designates a wild animal that impresses with its size and majesty, such as the lion or the crocodile. It is an animal of stately bearing, inspiring respect or fear. In Job 28:8, the "proud beasts" that even the lion does not dare to tread upon evoke the most formidable and majestic creatures of the animal kingdom.

2. Figuratively, the word emphasizes arrogance and domination: these animals impose their authority through their brute strength. In Job 41:25, the Leviathan is described as "the king of proud beasts," asserting its absolute superiority over all creatures. The term highlights less beauty than pride and untamability.
H7830.origine: The Hebrew word שַׁחַץ (shachats) expresses the idea of pride, haughty dignity, or majesty. It belongs to a family of Hebrew words related to pride and elevation. The base image is that of a creature that stands tall, imposing its presence through its stature and strength. This is why the word naturally applies to the greatest predators or wild beasts that reign unrivaled in nature.
H7830.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in Job, a book where divine power and wisdom surpass every creature. In Job 28:8, it qualifies the most fearsome wild animals, those that even the lion spares. In Job 41:25, it crowns the Leviathan, a mythical creature of chaos and extreme power, as the undisputed sovereign of all proud beasts. These two usages underscore the immensity of divine power: if these splendid creatures are so terrifying, how much greater are the mysteries of God Himself.
H7830.portee: This word invites us to meditate on the power of creation and the limits of what is "great" in the eyes of the world. Proud beasts embody a force that one believes to be untamable, yet they are merely creatures under the gaze of God. For the believer, this relativizes human pride and reminds us that true majesty belongs only to the Creator.

sens: City in the territory of Issachar in ancient Israel
H7831.detail: Schachatsima was a small locality located in the territory of Issachar, one of the twelve tribes of Israel. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, during the description of the borders and cities assigned to Issachar after the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 19:22). It was situated between known localities such as Tabor and Beth-Shemesh.
H7831.origine: The name "Schachatsima" literally means "toward the heights" in Hebrew. It likely describes the geographical situation of the place, located in a mountainous or elevated region of the territory of Issachar. The suffix "-ima" or "-imah" is a common ending for place names in Hebrew.
H7831.emploi: Schachatsima is cited only once in the Old Testament, in Joshua 19:22, where it appears in the official list of cities assigned to the tribe of Issachar during the division of the promised land after the conquest led by Joshua. This precise enumeration of borders and cities was important to clearly identify the territories of each tribe and guarantee their inheritance.

sens: Laughing with mockery or disdain
Playing, dancing, having fun
Making music or entertainment
Rejoicing, having light-hearted fun
H7832.detail:
1. Laughing with mockery or disdain: this is a laugh that expresses contempt or insolence toward someone. The Lord's animal "laughs" in disdain of men's weapons (Job 41:20), and God "laughs" at the plots of the wicked (Psalms 2:4).
2. Playing, dancing, having fun: the word denotes the action of making joyful or playful gestures, such as dancing before God. King David "dances" enthusiastically when the ark enters Jerusalem (1 Chronicles 15:29).
3. Making music or entertainment: "playing" instruments, singing, dancing together in a festive or celebratory context. David "plays" the harp before Saul (1 Samuel 18:7), and the musicians "play" their instruments during the feast (1 Chronicles 13:8).
4. Rejoicing, having light-hearted fun: the leviathan "plays" in the waves (Psalms 104:26), evoking a joyful and carefree freedom.
H7832.origine: The root primarily means "to laugh" in the sense of mocking, with the idea of a strong and visible action. It also expresses the idea of "playing" or "dancing," that is, moving lightly and freely, without serious intent. In Hebrew, the word thus encompasses both mocking laughter and playful joy — two expressions of the same movement of rejection or nonchalance.
H7832.emploi: The verb appears 36 times in the Hebrew Bible. It often denotes mocking or disdainful laughter: God "laughs" at his enemies (Psalms 2:4, 37:13), an animal "laughs" at the threat (Job 41:20). But it also expresses festive joy and entertainment: dancing and playing during religious celebrations (1 Chronicles 15:29), playing music (1 Samuel 18:7), or simply having fun without seriousness (Proverbs 26:19). In the Psalms and Jeremiah, "dancing" and "rejoicing" go together as signs of future messianic joy (Jeremiah 31:4). The context determines whether the laughter is mocking or joyful.
H7832.portee: This word shows two faces of biblical joy: the laughter of confidence of one who scorns threats (God who "laughs" at his enemies), and the exuberant joy of celebration and dancing before God. For the believer, it invites both not to fear the powers of evil and to celebrate God with a liberated joy, without restraint.

sens: Reduce to fine powder by grinding
Completely crush something solid
Annihilate an enemy (figuratively)
H7833.detail: 1. The verb describes the action of reducing a substance to fine powder by repeated grinding. In Exodus 30:36, incense is ground into powder for the sanctuary: it is a work of transformation, where something solid becomes fine dust. 2. More generally, it means to crush, pulverize what is hard or compact. Job 14:19 uses it for waters that grind down stone: patient water disintegrates and carries away even the hardest rock. 3. Applied to enemies (2 Samuel 22:43 and Psalms 18:43), the verb takes on a warrior and figurative value: one grinds his adversaries to dust, treads them down like mud, meaning one reduces them to nothing, completely crushing them.
H7833.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׁחַק comes from a root that evokes the action of rubbing, reducing by friction. The basic image is that of friction that disintegrates: a mill that grinds, water that wears down stone. This same idea of gradual destruction through wear is found in other uses of the word in the ancient Near East.
H7833.emploi: The verb appears four times in the Hebrew Bible (Exodus, 2 Samuel, Job, Psalms). In two cases (the incense, the stone), it describes a real physical transformation. In two others (2 Samuel 22:43 and Psalms 18:43, two parallel passages where David celebrates his victories), it is metaphorically applied to crushed enemies: the victorious warrior "grinds" his adversaries as one grinds grain or powder. It is the image of total victory, where the enemy is nothing but dust underfoot.
H7833.portee: This word reminds us that God can reduce to nothing the obstacles and enemies of his people. It also evokes the idea that transformation — even that which seems destructive — is part of God's design: the ground incense becomes purer and more fragrant, the crushed enemies liberate the people. For the believer, it is an assurance: in the face of powers that seem insurmountable, God has the strength to grind them like grain.

sens: Fine dust that rises in the air
Visible mass of water vapor in the sky
Veil or obscurity that hides the view
Divine majesty
Abundance or countless multitude
H7834.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes fine dust that floats in the air, almost imperceptible: it is this lightness, this tenuous and vaporous character that is its first image. 2. But it mainly applies to clouds that veil the sky: in Isaiah 40:15, the peoples are like the dust of the clouds, so tiny that God ignores them. 3. This veil that masks can also represent an obstacle or mystery: in Job 37:21, one cannot see the sun through the clouds, an image of what escapes our understanding. 4. In a higher register, the clouds become the throne or chariot of the Almighty God: in Deuteronomy 33:26, God "is carried on the clouds" with majesty, which manifests his glory. 5. The clouds can also symbolize immensity or multiplicity: in Job 38:37, only God can count the clouds, an expression of what exceeds number and surpasses human wisdom.
H7834.origine: The Hebrew word shachaq comes from a root that evokes the idea of fineness, crumbling, of what is tenuous and dissolves. It has the same meaning as the word that denotes "fine dust" or "floating dust": the image is that of light particles that float. This word, used in poems and hymns of praise, carries within it the sensation of lightness and immateriality, characteristic of the sky and what rises above the earthly world.
H7834.emploi: The word appears twenty-one times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms, the book of Job, and the Torah. It is often linked to God himself: either God acts through the clouds (he commands them in Psalms 78:23), or he is "carried" or "sitting" on them as on a throne, which expresses his cosmic royalty (Deuteronomy 33:26, Psalms 18:12). In Job, the word takes on a more philosophical hue: the clouds question human wisdom and ignorance, for neither Job nor the ordinary man can know their secrets (Job 36:28, 38:37). In a few rare occurrences (Isaiah 40:15), the clouds serve as a comparison to express the smallness or relative nothingness of earthly things before God. Its meaning thus glides from the concrete meteorological phenomenon to an expression of divine presence and mystery.
H7834.portee: This word invites the believer to contemplate the glory of God manifested in creation, particularly in what escapes human understanding and control. The clouds remind both of the majesty of the Lord, who walks in the invisible heights, and the humility that befits man, who knows so many secrets of God. For the psalmist who proclaims that God's faithfulness reaches "to the clouds," it is a word that lifts the gaze toward the divine and calls for trust in the one who rules over all elements.

sens: To become black or dark
To be burned, dried out by the sun or disease
H7835.detail:
1. The word literally refers to the change of color towards black, the darkening of the skin. In Job 30:30, Job describes how his skin "darkens": this is the result of his extreme suffering, illness, and exhaustion that transform his appearance.
2. In this same verse, the darkening of the skin goes hand in hand with his fall (it "falls") and the drying out of the bones: it is therefore less a cosmetic coloration than a visible sign of physical degradation, of the destruction of the body through suffering and evil.
H7835.origine: The Hebrew root שׁחר expresses the idea of blackness or darkening. It is related to the image of black, of darkness, and of what fades or alters. The word appears rarely in the Bible; it describes a visible process of transformation of the body, often linked to suffering or affliction.
H7835.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Job 30:30. Job uses it to paint the horror of his condition: abandoned by all, consumed by illness, his body bears the marks of his decay. The darkening of his skin is one symptom among others (fall, drying) of his physical and moral annihilation.
H7835.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that suffering leaves visible marks on our bodies and appearance. It invites us to recognize the gravity of Job's distress and not to minimize it—his complaint is not only spiritual but deeply physical. It is a call to compassion towards those who suffer.

sens: To search for something or someone carefully and diligently
To seek God, to address Him with prayers and desire
To actively pursue a goal or quality
H7836.detail:
1. The Hebrew verb שָׁחַר (sha.char) primarily means to actively and attentively seek something. The image is that of a meticulous search, often at dawn (hence sometimes "to seek early"). In Job 24:5, we see wild donkeys going out in the morning to seek food—this is the same diligent quest, this attentive inspection of a territory to find what one desires.

2. The Bible applies this verb to the search for God Himself. In Isaiah 26:9, the psalmist says: "My soul longs for You in the night, and my spirit seeks You within me"—this is a cry of the heart, a spiritual quest. In Job 7:21 and Job 8:5, seeking God means turning to Him earnestly, asking for His forgiveness or help.

3. The word can also refer to the search for a quality or result. In Proverbs 11:27: "He who seeks good attracts favor"—to seek good is to actively pursue it, to make it one's goal. It is a voluntary and sustained effort.
H7836.origine: The root שׁ-ח-ר (sh-ch-r) likely has the primary image of the rising of the day, of dawn (shachar = dawn, in Hebrew). To seek at dawn is to seek diligently, without delay, with all the energy of the morning. The verb exists in two main forms: the simple form (Qal), "to seek" or "to inspect", and the intensive form (Piel), "to seek ardently, to seek early". This intensity of the search at dawn is key: one rises early to seek, thus one truly seeks, tirelessly.
H7836.emploi: The verb appears about a dozen times in the Old Testament, especially in the Wisdom literature (Job, Proverbs, Psalms) and among the prophets. In Job, seeking God or turning to Him often follows a trial: Job 8:5 invites to "seek God" after suffering, implied to obtain His forgiveness. Proverbs uses the verb to seek good, wisdom, favor—always speaking of an active and rewarded quest (Proverbs 11:27). Psalm 63:2 and Isaiah 26:9 show the search for God as a nocturnal, spiritual, intimate desire. In Hosea 5:15, God says that His people will seek Him when they recognize their guilt. The word always emphasizes effort, sincere intention, and often urgency.
H7836.portee: This verb reminds the believer that the relationship with God requires an active search on the part of man, not a passive waiting. One only finds God if one seeks Him. The word also indicates that this spiritual quest is "natural"—just as one seeks food or survival, one must seek God with the same sincerity and perseverance. It is an invitation not to delay, to rise early spiritually to meet the Lord.

sens: The moment of day when the sun rises and night ends
The precise instant when the first light of morning appears
Figuratively, a new or glorious event that rises
The moment when something important or decisive begins
H7837.detail:
1. Dawn is the moment when night gives way to the light of day, when the sun appears on the horizon. It is this point in time when a new day begins. Genesis 19:15 refers to it as the moment when the angels urge Lot to leave Sodom before judgment.
2. It can refer to the precise instant, the nascent dawn, this fragile moment when light begins to break. Psalm 108:3 calls for dawn to awaken, as if it were a living force being summoned at daybreak.
3. Figuratively, dawn represents a glorious or new event that emerges. Isaiah 14:12 calls Satan the "morning star," evoking a light that rises—a original beauty before the fall.
4. It marks a turning point in history or destiny: Hosea 10:15 states that dawn will bring the end of the king of Israel, a moment of judgment and turning.
H7837.origine: The Hebrew word שַׁחַר (shachar) comes from a root that expresses the idea of awakening or emerging, of rising from darkness. It is the image of a clarity that is born and rises. The word is used to denote this concrete moment of the beginning of the day, and also to evoke everything that emerges, awakens, or begins to shine—hence its figurative use for new or glorious events.
H7837.emploi: The word appears 24 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Psalms and prophetic books. It designates both the material moment of daybreak (Genesis 32:24 where Jacob wrestles with the angel until dawn), and a decisive moment in an event (Joshua 6:15, the taking of Jericho which begins at dawn). In Job (38:12), God questions the patriarch asking if he has ever commanded the morning and shown its place to dawn: it is dawn as a wonder of divine creation. Among the prophets, dawn becomes a symbol of a turning point, of a divine intervention that emerges like light from the night.
H7837.portee: For the believer, dawn reminds us that each day is a new gift, a light that rises after the night. It also symbolizes how God acts: He brings change, justice, restoration, as light dispels darkness. It invites us to welcome what God brings forth, even when everything still seems dark.

sens: Black color, the absence or absorption of light
