Black complexion or skin
Black hair
Black horses or those with black coats
H7838.detail:
1. Black is the darkest color, the opposite of white and light. It is a shade that absorbs light rather than reflecting it. The Bible uses this word to concretely describe objects or beings of this color, without any value judgment (Zechariah 6:2 speaks of black horses harnessed to a chariot in a vision).
2. Black skin or dark complexion is described in Song of Solomon 1:5, where the author says, "I am black, but I am beautiful" — the blackness of the skin does not diminish beauty, a revolutionary idea for the time.
3. Black hair is typically associated with healthy and youthful hair. In Leviticus 13:31 and 13:37, the appearance or persistence of black hairs around a leprous sore is a sign of healing: the black hair indicates that life is returning to the diseased skin. Song of Solomon 5:11 compares the beloved's curls to the blackness of a raven, evoking beauty and brilliance.
4. A black horse is an animal with a black coat. Zechariah 6:6 mentions black horses harnessed to chariots, in the context of a prophetic vision of divine powers moving in the world.
H7838.origine: The Hebrew word שָׁחֹר comes from a root that simply denotes the color black, darkness. Its image is that of the absence of light. There is no complex etymology: it is the ordinary and universal word for this shade in biblical Hebrew. The Bible uses only one word for black, unlike Greek or other languages that may have nuances.
H7838.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the provided Hebrew Bible, always as an adjective describing the color of something or someone. Four usages concern the human or animal body: hair, skin, horses. Two usages are in Leviticus 13, a ritual text on leprosy: the black of the hairs is a medical criterion for healing, as it shows that the skin has regained its vitality. Two usages are found in Song of Solomon, where black describes beauty: the beloved's black skin and the beloved's black hair. Finally, two usages belong to Zechariah 6, where the black horses are actors in a symbolic vision of God's forces. In all cases, the word remains descriptive, without moral connotation: blackness is neutral, sometimes even praised.
H7838.portee: This word reminds us that the color black, in the Bible, is never despised or associated with evil — unlike later traditions. Black skin is beautiful; black hair is a sign of health and youth. This biblical simplicity frees the Christian reader from any negative association based on skin color. It also invites us to see how the Bible describes beings with sobriety: it says what it sees, without judgment.

sens: The dark or black hue of hair
Youth or physical vigor in bloom
H7839.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes darkness, particularly that of hair — this beautiful natural dark color of youth, which contrasts with the graying of hair in old age. 2. By extension, it symbolizes youth itself in its strength and beauty, the time when one has black hair and is overflowing with vitality. This is the sense seen in Ecclesiastes 12:2, where the wise man enumerates the vanities of life: "Remove sorrow from your heart, and put away evil from your flesh; for childhood and the dawn are vanity." Here, "dawn" symbolizes that entire period of youth and health that passes quickly, which is but vanity.
H7839.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes darkness and obscurity. The image is that of black hair of youth, a biblical symbol of strength and beauty that wears away with time. This association between black hair and vigorous youth appears throughout Scripture.
H7839.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Ecclesiastes 12:2, in the context of the passage where the Preacher enumerates the futility of youth. It is juxtaposed with "youth" and presented as a human vanity, a beauty and strength that fade with time. The word conveys the abstract concept of youth through the concrete image of black hair.
H7839.portee: This verse invites the believer not to cling too much to the beauty and youth of the body, which are only temporary. It encourages placing one's heart elsewhere than in physical pride or fleeting carnal pleasures, and finding wisdom that lasts forever.

sens: Black or very dark color of the skin
Sunburned or tanned appearance
H7840.detail:
1. The word denotes the black or very dark color, particularly that of human skin. In Song of Solomon, the young girl pleads with her lover not to judge her by her appearance: "Do not look upon me because I am dark" (Song of Solomon 1:6). She explains that this darkness comes from the burning sun that has exposed her as a vineyard keeper.
2. It is therefore an acquired darkness, that of tan and sunburn caused by prolonged exposure to the sun. The image evokes outdoor work, physical fatigue, and the elements: the sun has changed the natural color of her skin. This detail reveals something about her social status (agricultural worker) and her humility.
H7840.origine: The Hebrew word is formed from the root שׁחר (shaar), which carries the idea of black, dark, that which is obscured. It is an intensive or reduplicated adjective (as seen in its structure: she-char-cho-ret), which reinforces the idea: very black, very dark, intensely dark. The same root gives rise to other words denoting black, darkness, or obscurity.
H7840.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Song of Solomon 1:6. The young girl who sings this song explains to her listeners that her skin is not naturally black, but has become black or very dark due to sun exposure. This is a specific trait in this context: a poetic love dialogue where the heroine defends her beauty despite her tanned complexion. The word paints a contrast: between her deep nature (which she may imagine to be lighter) and her current appearance transformed by work and the sun.
H7840.portee: This verse invites the reader to look beyond outward appearances. The beauty and worth of a person are not reduced to their complexion or physique. The young girl in Song of Solomon teaches humility and confidence: she accepts what the sun has done to her skin, and she asks her beloved to see beyond this appearance. It is a call to true love, which looks at the heart and not just the surface.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the divided monarchy
H7841.detail: Schecharia is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, at a time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between North and South. His name means "dawn of the Lord" or "the Lord rises." He was the son of Jeroham and brother to several other men: Shamsherai, Athalia, Jaareshiah, Elie, and Zichri. He appears in the genealogy of the Benjamites, which shows how the families of this tribe have perpetuated through generations.
H7841.origine: The name Schecharia comes from Hebrew and is composed of two elements: "shechar" (dawn, morning) and "yah" (abbreviation of the divine name Yahweh, the Lord). It is therefore a theophoric name, meaning it incorporates the name of God. This reflects a common practice among Benjamites and other Israelites to form proper names by including a reference to God, thus expressing a dependence on Him or a prayer at the time of birth.
H7841.emploi: Schecharia appears only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 8:26, in the genealogical list of the sons of Jeroham. This passage enumerates the descendants of Benjamin and affirms the renewal and continuity of this tribe. The context shows that the tribe of Benjamin, despite the political troubles of the divided monarchy, maintained its family and genealogical structures, which the chronicler carefully preserved.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the divided monarchy
H7842.detail: Schacharaïm is a man of the tribe of Benjamin whose genealogy is listed in the register of Benjaminite families. He lived during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided. According to 1 Chronicles 8:8, he had several wives — Hushim, Baara, and Hodesh — and many sons: Jobab, Zibia, Mesha, Malcam, Jeuz, Sachia, Mirmah, Abitub, and Elpaal. The text indicates that he had children in the land of Moab after sending away his first two wives.
H7842.origine: The name Schacharaïm means "double dawn" in Hebrew: it comes from the root שׁחר (shachar, "dawn") doubled to form a plural or an intensive. It is a descriptive name that evokes the rising dawn, perhaps chosen for its bright or symbolic character.
H7842.emploi: Schacharaïm appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:8. He is mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Benjamin, one of Jacob's twelve sons. His name appears in a genealogical list intended to establish family ties within the tribe, suggesting that he held a recognized place in the genealogical history of Israel. The context indicates that he had withdrawn to the land of Moab, a territory east of the Jordan.

sens: Physically damage, ruin a material thing
Annihilate through violence, destroy a person or a people
Rot, decompose, cause natural degradation
Morally alter, pervert the heart or behavior
Spoil, ruin the quality or integrity of something
H7843.detail:
1. Physically damage or ruin a material thing: the word refers to the damage caused to an object, a building, or property. Thus in Lamentations 2:8, the Lord "destroys the walls of the daughter of Zion."

2. Annihilate through violence, kill or destroy a people: this is the action of completely destroying a person or group. In 1 Samuel 26:15, David asks Abner why he did not guard the king, "for someone from the people came to kill the king." In Genesis 6:17, God says: "I will destroy all living beings."

3. Rot, decompose: the image of natural rot, degradation over time. This is what happens to dead flesh or abandoned crops.

4. Pervert or morally corrupt: alter the heart and behavior of people. In Genesis 6:11-12, "the earth was corrupt before God, the earth was full of violence." This corruption is a deviation from the right path, an adoption of evil practices.

5. Spoil or degrade the quality of something: compromise the integrity or usefulness of something. In Deuteronomy 4:31, the Lord will not "destroy" His people, meaning He will not definitively spoil them.
H7843.origine: The root שׁחת (sha.chat) evokes the fundamental idea of damage and degradation, whether physical or moral. It belongs to a family of Hebrew words describing ruin and destruction. The cognate Aramaic she.chat (שְׁחַת) carries the same meaning. This verb encompasses both the action of actively destroying and the state of what is destroyed or rotten.
H7843.emploi: This verb appears 135 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Genesis (the flood, the destruction of Sodom), Exodus, the historical books, and the prophets. Its meaning varies according to context and grammatical construction. Physically, it describes the destruction of cities, walls, and crops (Lamentations 2:8, 2 Chronicles 36:19). In a moral and religious sense, it characterizes the corruption of the heart and ways of men (Genesis 6:11-12, Isaiah 1:4). God can also be the subject: He "destroys" those who defy Him or reject His covenant (Deuteronomy 4:31, 2 Chronicles 35:21). The word can also qualify a person — "destroyer" — one who causes ruin (Jeremiah 2:30).
H7843.portee: This word reminds the reader of the reality of destruction and corruption—both physical and moral—that characterize a world separated from God. It highlights God's judgment in the face of rebellion and evil, but also His mercy when He restrains His destructive hand. For the believer, it invites self-examination: am I corrupted by sin, or kept pure by grace?

sens: Word or statement contrary to the truth
Deliberate lie or deception
Corruption of the true by the false
H7844.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes what is false, inaccurate, contrary to reality — a word that does not tell the truth. In Daniel 2:9, the king's magicians are accused of wanting to speak "falsehoods," meaning lies to deceive Nebuchadnezzar about the content of his dream.
2. It is also the voluntary lie, the intention to deceive by word. Those who seek to corrupt or harm use falsehood as a weapon: according to Daniel 6:4, no "falsehood" is found in Daniel's conduct, meaning he cannot be faulted, that there is nothing deceptive or corrupt in him.
H7844.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to corrupt" or "to spoil." It denotes what is damaged, altered, deviated from its true nature — falsehood corrupts truth as a rotten thing corrupts what is healthy. The root evokes the image of deterioration: just as one corrupts an object by degrading it, one corrupts the truth by distorting it through lies.
H7844.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament according to the Vulgate and ancient versions, but only once clearly attested in Daniel 2:9. Its meaning is that of lie or deceptive word. In Daniel 2:9, it qualifies the false explanations that the magicians would want to invent. In Daniel 6:4, it describes the absence of guilt or malice in Daniel's life — there is nothing false or corrupt to blame him for. The word thus emphasizes both the deceptive intention and the corrupted result: one who utters a falsehood seeks to distort the truth to deceive.
H7844.portee: This word reminds us that in God's eyes, lies and deception are not mere errors, but a corruption — a degradation of the truth itself. It invites the believer to honor the truth in words and actions, like Daniel who never gave cause for accusations of falsehood. It is a call to integral honesty, a fruit of the fear of God.

sens: Excavation dug in the ground, especially a grave or well
Abyss or chasm, an image of death and destruction
The abode of the dead, the afterlife
Corruption and decomposition of the body
H7845G.detail:
1. The pit primarily refers to an excavation dug in the ground: a grave, a well, or any deep hollow. This is the most concrete meaning of the word. In Job 33:28, it speaks of not entering the pit, which means not descending into the grave.

2. The word also evokes an abyss or chasm, a fall downward that symbolizes death and destruction. It is a strong image: falling into a pit means disappearing, perishing. Psalms 49:10 states that men "will not escape the sight of the pit," meaning they cannot escape death.

3. The pit becomes the name for the abode of the dead, equivalent to Sheol. It is the place one descends to when they die, the dreaded afterlife. Psalms 30:10 cries out: "What profit is there in my blood, to bring me down to the pit?"

4. The word can also refer to the corruption, the decomposition of the corpse in the grave. Psalms 16:10 says, "You will not allow Your holy one to see corruption," meaning that the body will not decompose in the tomb.
H7845G.origine: The Hebrew word sha.chat comes from a root meaning "to dig" or "to make an excavation." It evokes the primary image of a hollow, a hole in the ground. In the Old Testament, this word gradually becomes synonymous with Sheol, the abode of the dead in Hebrew understanding: both a physical grave and a realm of death. The Septuagint (an ancient Greek translation) often translates it as "pit" or "abyss."
H7845G.emploi: This word appears thirteen times in the Old Testament, primarily in Psalms and Job, which deal with death and divine salvation. In Job 33, it refers to the mortal danger from which God can deliver the righteous. The Psalms often use it to express the fear of dying and descending to the abode of the dead, but also to celebrate divine deliverance: "God has delivered my soul from going down to the pit" (Job 33:28). In the prophets (Isaiah, Ezekiel, Jonah), the pit represents imminent destruction or judgment. The word thus oscillates between its concrete meaning of grave or excavation and its spiritual meaning of death and perdition.
H7845G.portee: For the believer, this word reminds that the pit—death and perdition—is a daunting reality, but that only God can deliver from it. The Psalms celebrate this deliverance as an act of divine mercy: God "delivers your life from the pit." It is a word of hope for those who fear death: it is not inevitable if God intervenes. This theme also prepares the Christian mystery: the one whom God loves will not see corruption (Psalms 16:10, interpreted messianically), a promise fulfilled in the resurrected Jesus Christ.

sens: Hole dug in the ground, deep and often covered, used to trap or imprison
Quagmire, muck, viscous substance in which one sinks
Tomb, burial place, where the dead rest
Image of destruction, perdition, or mortal danger
H7845H.detail:
1. A pit is a hole excavated, intentionally dug to capture animals or enemies—a deadly trap. In Psalms 7:16, the one who "opens a pit, digs it" secretly prepares his own ruin: what he intended for others overtakes him.
2. The pit can also be a slimy, muddy substance: in Job 9:31, Job says that God would "plunge him into the mire"—an image of total defilement and humiliation, where all hope of purity sinks away.
3. The pit refers to the sepulcher, the dwelling of the dead. In Job 17:14, in his despair, Job addresses the "pit" as if it were his father, and the worms as his family—he contemplates his own death.
4. More broadly, it is the image of inevitable misfortune, destruction, or impending death: in Job 33:22, "the soul draws near to the pit" when death threatens.
H7845H.origine: The Hebrew word שַׁחַת (shachat) primarily denotes a hole dug in the ground. Its root evokes the action of digging, excavating. In the Old Testament, it is used for the concrete traps set for wild animals, then for graves and chasms. It is a word of very concrete imagery: the Bible constantly uses the language of the body and matter to speak of spiritual realities, and the pit is a perfect example of this.
H7845H.emploi: The word "pit" (shachat) appears ten times in the Old Testament, mainly in Job and the Psalms. It first denotes physical traps: in Psalms 35:7, enemies dig a pit to take life. But it quickly becomes metaphorical: Job invokes it as synonymous with the sepulcher and imminent death. The Psalms use it as the image of punishment received (Psalms 9:16: "the nations fall into the pit they have made"). It is a word of poetic and sapiential language, rare in narratives and absent from the Gospels.
H7845H.portee: The pit reminds the reader that our wicked actions prepared against others come back to reach us—it is the wisdom of Ecclesiastes and the Psalms. It also symbolizes the power of death and sin, hence the call to justice and mercy from God. It is a terrifying yet clear image: it shows the concrete reality of divine judgment and our responsibilities before Him.

sens: one who deviates from the right path, who turns away from the law
one who acts wickedly, who commits reprehensible acts
one who willingly sinks into evil and crime
H7846.detail:
1. The word literally designates someone who "deviates" or "turns aside"—not by accident or ignorance, but by a deliberate choice not to follow the right path. It is a very concrete image: the sinner is one who voluntarily abandons the good road. In Psalm 101:3, the king affirms that he will not tolerate the presence of such deviants near him: "I hate the conduct of sinners."
2. More broadly, it refers to one who "sinks" into evil, who persists in wicked acts. The Hebrew verb evokes the idea of sinking deeply, as into a chasm. In Hosea 5:2, the unfaithful "sink into crime" through their hypocritical sacrifices: they dig their own ruin.
3. Finally, it is a conduct characterized by rebellion against the order established by God—not just an isolated fault, but a habitual attitude of one who deliberately refuses to obey.
H7846.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to deviate," "to turn aside," "to leave the path." It is a very ancient image in the vocabulary of the Old Testament: the sinner is not primarily one who stumbles, but one who chooses to turn elsewhere. This root also appears in other forms to express the idea of deviation or rebellion. The underlying image is that of a marked path, a direction to follow—and of one who voluntarily strays from it.
H7846.emploi: This word is rare in the Hebrew Bible: only two occurrences are preserved. In Psalm 101:3, it describes those who deviate from the right path, whose conduct is wicked—the king promises to distance himself from them. In Hosea 5:2, the context shows how the unfaithful "sink" progressively into crime, each of their acts plunging them deeper into sin. Both uses emphasize the voluntary and progressive nature of deviation: it is a repeated choice, not a mere fall.
H7846.portee: This word reminds the reader that sin is not a fate imposed from the outside, but a voluntary turning away from the right path. It invites us to examine our own choices: do we remain on the path that God has shown us, or do we stray from it? The image of sinking into evil also shows that each wicked act sinks us further—hence the urgency to return to the right path.

sens: Change direction, stray from the path
Abandon, leave what was secure or established
Transgress, step out of obedience
Commit marital infidelity
H7847.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to turn away means to turn one's face or body elsewhere, to stray from the path one was following. In Proverbs 4:15, it is commanded to turn away from a strange woman: do not pass by where she is, but take another path.
2. The verb takes on a moral significance: to turn away means to abandon what was established or secure, to step out of authority or protection. In Numbers 5:19, "under the power of your husband" and "you have not turned away" describe the wife who remains faithful, staying under his authority.
3. To turn away can mean to transgress, to disobey: in Proverbs 7:25, it refers to not letting one's heart "turn away" toward the ways of a strange woman, meaning not to be led into sin.
4. In Numbers 5:12, the context shows the most serious meaning: a woman "turning away from her husband" means she commits adultery, she strays from her marital covenant to defile herself with another.
H7847.origine: The Hebrew root means to turn, to deviate. It paints the image of a person turning their back, changing direction. In the Old Testament, this verb first describes concrete movements, then becomes an image of infidelity or disobedience.
H7847.emploi: The verb appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in Numbers 5 (4 occurrences) in the law concerning the suspicion of adultery, where it describes the unfaithful wife who "turns away" from her husband. The verses in Proverbs 4 and 7 use the same verb in a moral sense: do not let yourself be turned away toward evil, toward the paths of the strange woman. The meaning thus shifts from marital infidelity to moral transgression in general.
H7847.portee: This word reminds us that infidelity, whether marital or spiritual, is primarily a "turning away": one turns their back on the one to whom they were committed. For the Christian, it invites one to remain attached to what is established—marriage, faithfulness to God—and not to be drawn elsewhere.

sens: Tree of North Africa and the Middle East, with hard and durable wood
Wood from this tree, used in construction
H7848.detail:
1. The acacia is a tropical tree that grows in the warm and arid regions of the Middle East and North Africa. Its wood is extremely hard, dense, and rot-resistant, making it valuable for durable constructions. It is a golden-colored wood that ages well.
2. This wood was the primary material for the tabernacle and all its sacred furniture. God commanded Moses: "You shall make an ark of acacia wood" (Exodus 25:10), as well as the table of showbread (Exodus 37:10), the altar of incense (Exodus 37:25), and the altar of burnt offerings (Exodus 38:1). The poles intended to carry these furnishings were also made of acacia (Exodus 25:28), as were the vertical boards of the tabernacle structure (Exodus 36:20).
H7848.origine: The Hebrew word שִׁטָּה (shittah) refers to this particular tree, scientifically known as Acacia nilotica or tortilis. Its name likely comes from a root meaning wood or its hardness. It is a term specifically Middle Eastern and biblical. In the Old Testament, it only appears in contexts related to the tabernacle and its accessories, indicating that it was the preferred wood for sacred items.
H7848.emploi: This word appears 28 times in the Bible, almost exclusively in the books of Exodus and Deuteronomy, during the detailed description of the tabernacle and its furnishings. It is also found once in Isaiah (41:19) where God promises to plant acacias in the desert. In all uses related to the tabernacle, the acacia wood is systematically covered with gold or associated with gold (Exodus 25:28, 26:37), symbolizing the union of wood (earthly, human) and gold (divine, heavenly). It is the chosen wood par excellence for everything that served the worship of the true God.
H7848.portee: God's choice of acacia wood for the tabernacle teaches that God uses the material available in creation, even humble, for His service. The acacia, an ordinary wood from the Sinai desert, became precious when destined for the worship of God. This reminds us that our life, even ordinary and earthly, becomes sacred when it is dedicated to God.

sens: deploy, open something flat widely
lay flat on a surface
increase in extent, enlarge
raise, stretch toward
H7849.detail:
1. To extend means to unfold or spread something in a way that makes it flat and spread out. Quails are spread out on the ground around the camp to dry (Numbers 11:32), and the threshed grain is spread over a well to conceal its opening (2 Samuel 17:19).
2. To thresh grain means to crush or grind it: the word refers to both the action of reducing to crumbs and the result — crushed grain in fine powder.
3. To extend far means also to enlarge, to prosper: this is what God does to the nations He wants to multiply (Job 12:23), showing that the word applies to expansion, to the increase of influence and territory.
4. Extending hands toward God means stretching them out to Him in a gesture of supplication or appeal (Psalms 88:10) — the image is one of opening palms, presenting one's hands to someone.
5. To extend the dead before the sun means to expose them to the sight of all, to dishonor them by leaving them unburied (Jeremiah 8:2) — an image of humiliation and abandonment.
H7849.origine: The Hebrew root שׁטח expresses the idea of deploying, spreading widely. It evokes the gesture of taking something soft or compact and making it flat and extended — like unfolding a garment or spreading dough. The word describes the concrete action of transforming a volume into a surface.
H7849.emploi: This verb appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts where it is about making visible, spreading out, or enlarging. In the concrete sense, it describes the spreading of quails and grain (Numbers, 2 Samuel). In a broader sense, it expresses the expansion of nations and territories (Job), and it takes on a tone of supplication or appeal when referring to stretching out hands (Psalms). Finally, it can also mean humiliating exposure (Jeremiah). Each occurrence reinforces the idea of visible and public deployment.
H7849.portee: This word shows us that prayer is not hidden or shameful: extending hands toward God is an open and trusting gesture, like opening one's hands to receive (Psalms 88:10). It also reminds us that the extension of nations and empires — their visible greatness — remains in the hands of God alone, who raises and lowers them according to His will (Job 12:23).

sens: Instrument of punishment or control, generally composed of a strap or several cords attached to a handle
Figuratively, that which wounds, torments, or afflicts like a whip
H7850.detail:
1. The whip is literally an instrument made of cords or straps, used to strike and punish. It is an object of pain and physical control. In the Bible, it symbolizes divine or human punishment.

2. Figuratively, the whip represents any affliction that torments and wounds relentlessly. In Joshua 23:13, God warns Israel: the remaining nations will be for him "a whip on the sides," meaning a constant source of suffering and tribulation, as if they were striking him incessantly.
H7850.origine: The Hebrew word שֹׁטֵט comes from a root that evokes the action of striking or beating. It is in the same family as other Hebrew words related to punishment and correction. The image of the whip, an instrument of striking, captures well the idea of a force that wounds and dominates.
H7850.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Joshua 23:13. Joshua, at the end of his life, warns Israel that if they do not completely drive out the remaining peoples of Canaan, they will become a permanent source of suffering for him—a net, a trap, a whip on the sides, thorns in the eyes. It is a prophetic threat: disobedience to God's command will lead to constant affliction, like that caused by a whip.
H7850.portee: This verse reminds the Christian that disobedience to God does not bring peace, but affliction. The "whip" symbolizes the consequences of our spiritual compromises: they do not disappear, but torment us continually. It is a call to separation from what offends God and to total obedience, rather than to accommodations that wound us in the long term.

sens: Plain region in Transjordan, east of the Jordan
Campsite of the Israelites before entering Canaan
Acacias, trees of this region
H7851G.detail: 1. Shittim is a plain region located in Transjordan, that is, east of the Jordan, in the territory that the Israelites had already conquered. The name literally means "the acacias" in reference to the trees that grew there. 2. It is where Israel camps after the conquest of Transjordan and before crossing the Jordan to enter Canaan proper (Joshua 3:1). It is also the starting point from which Joshua sends the two spies to scout Jericho (Joshua 2:1). 3. The passage in Numbers 25:1 shows that it is at Shittim that the people fall into idolatry and debauchery with the Moabites, a serious event that provokes God's anger. Micah 6:5 refers to the path from Shittim to Gilgal as a testimony of the Lord's benefits to His people.
H7851G.origine: The Hebrew name "Shittim" (שִׁטִּים) comes from the word "shittah" which designates the acacia, a thorny tree of the desert capable of withstanding the arid climate. The plural "Shittim" literally means "the acacias." This name recalls the characteristic vegetation of this region of the Transjordanian highlands.
H7851G.emploi: Shittim is mentioned four times in the Bible, all in the context of Israel's last encampment before entering Canaan. In Numbers 25:1, it is the site of the people's grave sin with the Moabites. In Joshua 2:1, Shittim is the starting point for the mission of the spies sent to scout Jericho. In Joshua 3:1, the Israelites leave it to head toward the Jordan. Micah 6:5 mentions it as a landmark of the miraculous journey from Shittim to Gilgal, marking God's protective hand.
H7851G.portee: Shittim reminds us that even on the eve of the promised victory, God's people can fall into sin and idolatry. It is a place of contrast: on one side, Israel's grave unfaithfulness; on the other, God's faithfulness that continues His plan of salvation despite His people's sin. The journey from Shittim to Gilgal becomes a sign of the wonders accomplished by the Lord for His people.

sens: Valley in Judea, mentioned in the prophetic vision of Joel
H7851H.detail: Shittim is a valley located in Judea, west of Jerusalem. The name literally means "the acacias," trees that grew in this region. In the prophetic vision of Joel, this valley becomes the symbol of a restored and fruitful land: a spring will flow from the house of the Lord and water it, while the wine will flow down from the mountains and milk will flow from the hills (Joel 3:18). This valley thus represents the divine abundance promised to God's people in the messianic days.
H7851H.origine: The Hebrew name Shittim comes from the root meaning "acacia," the characteristic tree of this region. This valley is named after the vegetation that marks it, which is common in biblical toponymy. The wood of acacia is mentioned elsewhere in Scripture for the construction of the Tabernacle and its furnishings (Exodus 35:24).
H7851H.emploi: Shittim appears only once in the Bible as a place name, in the prophecy of Joel 3:18. It is mentioned in the prophet's vision as the symbol of the future blessing of the land of Judah. This unique mention underscores its symbolic importance rather than its frequency: Joel chooses this valley to illustrate the eschatological transformation of the land, marking the transition from barrenness to abundance under God's blessing.
H7851H.portee: For the Christian reader, Shittim embodies in prophecy the hope of radical transformation. The valley named after a desert tree becomes the place where a divine spring bursts forth: it reminds us that only God can transform a barren land into a land of abundance. This prophetic image encourages the believer to await the complete renovation of the world promised by God in eschatological times.

sens: Nurture a lasting animosity against someone, hold a grudge
Relentlessly pursue someone with hostility, attack them without respite
Manifest enmity through concrete acts
H7852.detail:
1. The verb primarily denotes the act of conceiving and nurturing hatred towards someone—not a momentary outburst of anger, but an animosity that one retains, that one cultivates in the heart. Esau "conceived" hatred against Jacob (Genesis 27:41), a grudge linked to the loss of his blessing, which he kept to the point of plotting murder.
2. The word then describes the action of pursuing someone with this hatred, that is, to relentlessly harass them with hostility. The archers have "pursued" with their hatred the one they attacked (Genesis 49:23); Job declares that God "pursues" him in His fury and "fights" him (Job 16:9 and 30:21).
3. Enmity is manifested through aggressive acts: this is why the word can also denote concrete opposition, merciless attack. The enemies of the Psalmist "pursue" him with anger (Psalms 55:4), uniting hostile will with hostile action.
H7852.origine: The Hebrew verb שָׂטַם (satam) comes from a root that evokes the idea of retaining, holding in reserve—hence the image of a hatred that one retains, that one accumulates within oneself. It contrasts with sudden anger: it is a lasting, simmering animosity. The word belongs to the family of Hebrew terms describing deep and calculated enmity rather than fleeting outbursts.
H7852.emploi: The verb appears six times in the Old Testament, mostly at the beginning of Genesis and in the Psalms or Job. In Genesis 27:41, it depicts Esau's grudge—a thoughtful, remembered hatred, waiting for its moment. In Genesis 49:23 and 50:15, it describes the active hostility of those who relentlessly pursue someone. In the poems of Job (16:9, 30:21) and Psalm 55:4, the psalmist or prophet uses this verb to express the feeling of being pursued, harassed by relentless enmity. The context varies depending on whether the subject is human or divine, but the central idea remains: a hatred that one cultivates and acts upon.
H7852.portee: This word helps us discern the nature of hatred in the eyes of the Bible: it is not a mere fleeting feeling, but an orientation of the heart that one maintains and expresses through acts. It warns us of the danger of nurturing a grudge—of conceiving and cultivating hatred like Esau—because it can lead us astray and away from grace. Conversely, it shows us how God in the Psalms or Job can appear hostile to the one who suffers, inviting the believer not to judge God by appearances.

sens: One who opposes someone, who resists or fights against them
One who accuses someone in court or in accusation
Declared enemy, one who seeks harm to others
H7853.detail:
1. The word primarily designates one who stands against you, who actively opposes your plans or words. It is the adversary in a conflict: the psalmist's enemies "repay me evil for good" (Psalms 38:21), seeking to harm him because he pursues good.
2. The word takes on a legal nuance when it designates one who accuses: Satan stands before the angel of the Lord "to accuse him" (Zechariah 3:1), playing the role of the prosecutor who attacks in court.
3. More broadly, it is the resolute enemy who conspires against your life. The psalmist's adversaries "seek my ruin" (Psalms 71:13) and he prays for those who "speak maliciously of me" to be punished (Psalms 109:20).
H7853.origine: The verb comes from a root that originally means "to turn against" or "to stand in the way." It expresses the idea of making an obstacle, of blocking the path. The word is also used as a proper name: Satan, the great adversary of God and men, is named by this word which retains this sense of opposition and accusation.
H7853.emploi: The verb appears six times in the Old Testament, primarily in the Psalms (four occurrences) where the psalmist speaks of his human enemies who oppose him, then in Zechariah where Satan himself "accuses" Joshua the high priest. The context is always one of declared hostility, of opposition that seeks the harm of others. The meaning oscillates between the human adversary and the divine adversary, but the idea remains constant: one who stands against you with hostile intent.
H7853.portee: This word reminds the believer that they should not ignore the existence of real opponents — not only visible enemies, but also spiritual powers that are set against them. At the same time, the Psalms show that the believer can cry out to God in the face of their adversaries and await His justice. It is an invitation to recognize real conflicts, spiritual and human, without fear but with the certainty that God sees and acts.

sens: one who opposes someone or fights against them
one who resists a plan or action
declared or national enemy
one who accuses or denounces
malevolent spiritual power rebelling against God
H7854.detail:
1. In the most concrete sense, it is someone who actively opposes you: the angel of the Lord stands in the way of Balaam to "resist" him (Numbers 22:32), that is, to block his path and prevent him from continuing. The word designates one who makes an obstacle.

2. It is also the enemy in combat or in politics: a war chief asks that David be sent away "so that he is not an enemy to us in battle" (1 Samuel 29:4), and Solomon has peace when the Lord removes his "adversaries" and calamities (1 Kings 5:4). It is one who harms or is feared as a rival.

3. Moving to a more abstract sense, the word designates an accuser or opponent in a trial: in the book of Job, the figure of Satan presents himself before God to accuse him (Job 1:6-9), and in the vision of Zechariah, Satan is the accuser (Zechariah 3:1). It is one who denounces and opposes.

4. The full meaning of the word in a spiritual context: Satan is the personified power of evil, the adversary of God and His people par excellence. He opposes God's plan, accuses believers before the throne (Job 1-2), and seeks to lead them astray. He is the supernatural enemy working against salvation.
H7854.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to oppose" or "to block the way." It expresses the idea of someone standing against you, blocking your path. The same root produces derivatives that describe the act of resisting or making an obstacle. In the Old Testament, the term first designates ordinary human enemies before taking on its full theological weight: one who opposes God Himself and His people, and ultimately the personified figure of evil.
H7854.emploi: The word appears 23 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in narrative books, the Psalms, and prophetic poetry. In the early books (Numbers, Samuel, Kings), it describes concrete human adversaries: military foes, political rivals, national enemies. Gradually, particularly in the book of Job and the prophetic visions of Zechariah, it designates a spiritual creature, a supernatural adversary who opposes not a man but God Himself. Satan accuses Job of serving God only for selfish reasons (Job 1:9-11), receives permission to test him, and this figure becomes the biblical symbol of opposition to God's plan. From these usages, "Satan" becomes the proper name of the prince of darkness in biblical theology.
H7854.portee: Understanding Satan as "adversary" helps the Christian grasp that evil is not an abstract or impersonal force, but an active and intelligent power that opposes God and His people. The Bible describes him as accuser and seducer, which sheds light on how sin operates: he accuses us before God and leads us to doubt His grace. Recognizing what Satan is — a defeated enemy by Christ (Colossians 2:15) — frees the believer from fear and gives them vigilance and confidence to walk in faith.

sens: Complaint or reproach presented against someone
Manifest enmity or hostility
H7855.detail:
1. An accusation is a formal complaint addressed against a person, a denunciation of their actions or conduct. In Ezra 4:6, the adversaries of the Jews write an accusation against the inhabitants of Judah and Jerusalem to King Ahasuerus: they lodge a complaint, they officially denounce them to prevent them from rebuilding the Temple.
2. The word also evokes enmity, active hostility: it is not a simple disagreement, but an opposition marked by malice and the will to harm.
H7855.origine: The Hebrew word sitnah comes from the root stn which means "to oppose" or "to be an adversary." The same root produces the name Satan, literally "the adversary" or "one who opposes." Sitnah thus designates the hostile action, the opposition that has become accusation. This vocabulary of hostility and malice runs throughout the Bible.
H7855.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezra 4:6, in the context of the return from exile: the enemies of the Jews present a written accusation to the Persian king to hinder the reconstruction of the Temple. The context shows that this accusation is an act of political hostility, a coordinated attempt to harm the Jews. The word emphasizes the formal and official nature of this opposition: it is not a private quarrel, but a complaint presented to royal authority.
H7855.portee: This word reminds us that opposition to the people of God often takes the form of accusations before the powerful of the world. For the Christian reader, it invites recognition of how hostility to the faith manifests itself through complaints, slanders, or denunciations. It is also an invitation to vigilance: the enemies of God continually present accusations, but God remains the true judge.

sens: Name of the second well dug by Isaac in the valley of Gerar
H7856.detail: Sitna is the name that Isaac gave to the second well he dug in the valley of Gerar. The name means "quarrel" or "conflict" in Hebrew, as the local shepherds disputed with Isaac over the possession of this well, just as they had done for the first well he had dug (Genesis 26:21).
H7856.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew "sitna," which literally means "quarrel" or "hostility." Isaac chose this name to commemorate the conflict that arose over this well. The first well was named Esek ("quarrel"), and the second Sitna, both named after the disputes they caused.
H7856.emploi: Sitna appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 26:21. It is mentioned in the account where Isaac, settled in the valley of Gerar in the land of the Philistines, digs wells. Each well he digs provokes a dispute with the local shepherds, hence the significant names given to these wells. This context illustrates the tensions and rivalries that Isaac must face to secure his water resources.

sens: To flow with force and abundance, referring to water that spills out of its bed
To wash, rinse, clean with water
To be swept away, engulfed by an irresistible flow
To surge forward with impetuosity, to rush
To submerge, engulf, completely cover
To ravage, devastate violently
H7857.detail:
1. Overflow: water violently exits its normal course and spreads everywhere. This is the image of a river in flood, waters inundating everything in their path (Isaiah 28:17: "the waters will overflow the hiding place of lies").
2. To wash, rinse: to clean something by immersing or rubbing it with water. This is an ordinary gesture, like that of a clay vessel being washed (Leviticus 6:21) or hands being rinsed after contact with something unclean.
3. To be swept away: water seizes you and carries you away irresistibly, like crushed stone swept away by the current (Job 14:19). It is also the experience of the psalmist submerged by the waters (Psalms 69:3).
4. To surge forward, to rush: to advance with force and speed, without restraint, like a horse charging into battle (Jeremiah 8:6: "All return to their course, like a horse that rushes"). The image shifts from water to impetuous motion.
5. To completely submerge: to cover entirely, to weigh down, as love cannot be submerged by water (Song of Solomon 8:7).
6. To ravage, devastate: to forcefully pass through and destroy everything, like the violent rain and hail of judgment (Ezekiel 38:22: "I will rain down fire and brimstone").
H7857.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the violent and abundant movement of water. The same root is found in words related to water, flow, and impetuous action. The word first paints the concrete image of overflowing water, then extends to any action that engulfs, sweeps away, or submerges with power. The root emphasizes the idea of irresistible force and loss of control.
H7857.emploi: The verb appears about 30 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the prophetic (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel) and poetic (Psalms, Job) books. In its concrete sense, it denotes the overflow of waters (flooded rivers, inundations), ritual washing and cleaning (Leviticus). In its figurative sense, the Bible uses it to describe divine judgments that overwhelm the wicked like a devastating flood (Isaiah 28, Ezekiel 38), or to express the distress of the righteous submerged by misfortune (Psalms 69). In Jeremiah 8:6 and Daniel, the verb also describes the impetuous advance of an army. The word oscillates between the natural image and the warrior or divine image.
H7857.portee: This word reminds the believer of God's undeniable power: His judgments fall like an irresistible flood upon evil. But it also states that nothing—not even water, nor distress—can drown God's love for His people. Finally, the word invites spiritual vigilance: to refuse to be "overwhelmed" by sin and evil, just as one guards against violent waters.

sens: A passage or channel of flowing water
A violent overflow of water
A great number of things that flow or advance like water
An intense and irresistible demonstration of force or feeling
H7858.detail:
1. The word first designates a course or passage through which water flows: God has "opened a passage for the rain" that follows its path like lightning and thunder (Job 38:25).
2. It then describes the violent overflow of waters that spill out of their bed: "If great waters overflow," they will not reach the one who takes refuge in God (Psalms 32:6), for even a flood has no hold on him.
3. The word is also used for armies that spread out in mass: the "troops that will spread like a torrent" will nevertheless be overwhelmed and annihilated before a stronger leader (Daniel 11:22).
4. It finally characterizes any feeling or force that exerts itself with violence and power: jealousy is "impetuous"—it is as crushing and irrepressible as a flood (Proverbs 27:4).
H7858.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to flow" or "to pour out." It is an image of violent and continuous movement, that of water overflowing its bed and sweeping everything in its path. This uncontrollable movement applies both to the physical overflow of waters and to the striking power of an emotion or military force.
H7858.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in prophetic and poetic passages. Job uses it for the ways of water created by God. The Psalms and Proverbs use it to express threats or powers that descend. Daniel applies it to armies that surge and to destruction that comes like a flood. Nahum uses it to describe how God will destroy Nineveh with overflowing waves. The meaning thus varies between natural water, military crowds, and violent feelings, but always retains the idea of a force that overflows and sweeps away.
H7858.portee: This word reveals how the Bible uses the image of nature to speak of what escapes human control. For the believer, it reminds that the powers that seem irresistible—wars, emotions, disasters—are ultimately in God's hands. He alone opens or stops the passages of water, judges nations, and knows the outcome: the psalmist finds refuge and certainty for his faith.

sens: The flank or one of the two lateral surfaces of a body
Position to the left or right of something
H7859.detail:
1. The word designates the flank or lateral surface of a body, what one might touch by placing a hand on the side of a person or an animal. In Daniel's vision, the bear that rises "on one side" stands up leaning on one of its flanks, like an animal partially rising to threaten (Daniel 7:5).
2. More broadly, the side can indicate a lateral position, to the left or right of a reference point: it is the place that borders something rather than being at its center or forefront.
H7859.origine: The Hebrew word שְׂטַר comes from a root that expresses the idea of "side" or "lateral surface." It lies on the flank of a person or an animal. The root also appears in other Hebrew forms related to the notion of moving aside or placing to the side. This concrete notion of the flank or edge characterizes all the usage of the word in the Hebrew Bible.
H7859.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Daniel 7:5. The apocalyptic vision situates it in a description of a symbolic animal: the bear that stands on one side (rather than on all its limbs) represents a threatening and unstable posture. The context of Daniel's visions highlights the image of danger and imminence: the animal rises to strike. Its unique and remarkable usage makes it a rare word, reserved here to describe a symbolic posture.
H7859.portee: For the reader, this image of the bear rising on one side captures the threatening and unbalanced nature of worldly power in vision. It shows how God represents human empires as wild animals, raising the question: whom can I truly rely on? This description reminds that earthly political forces, however impressive they may seem, are creatures subject to God's vision and judgment.

sens: Person in charge of executing the orders of a higher authority
Administrative agent who supervises and oversees the people
Military or civil leader responsible for a division or duty
Local magistrate or judge
H7860.detail:
1. The officer is primarily one who receives orders and transmits them: in Egypt, Pharaoh's taskmasters receive the order to impose labor on the children of Israel (Exodus 5:6), and the Israelite taskmasters must convey it to the people (Exodus 5:19). They are a relay of power.
2. In the organization of the people of Israel, the officer supervises and maintains order: Moses appoints officers alongside the elders to assist in judging (Deuteronomy 1:15), and they are the ones who speak to the soldiers before battle (Deuteronomy 20:5). They serve as intermediaries between the leaders and the multitude.
3. In the army and administration of the king, the officer has a specific charge: in David's time, the officers serve the king in organizing military divisions (1 Chronicles 27:1), each commanding twenty-four thousand men.
4. The officer can also be a magistrate or local inspector tasked with enforcing the law: in Deuteronomy 16:18, he is appointed alongside the judge to administer justice in the cities.
H7860.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to make a judgment" or "to decree." The officer is one who "functions as" or "fills the role of" judge or commander. The family of words in Hebrew includes terms related to administration and charge.
H7860.emploi: This word appears 25 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Pentateuch (Exodus, Deuteronomy, Numbers) and in historical narratives (Joshua, Chronicles). In ancient Egypt, Pharaoh's taskmasters and Israelite taskmasters are faces of brutal power and forced labor. Later, in the Israelite organization under the law (Deuteronomy), the officer becomes a legal institution: Moses appoints officers to assist the judges and supervise the people. In the time of the kings, the officer is integrated into the military and administrative apparatus: David appoints them for each division. The word also appears in Proverbs 6:7, where the ant has no officer, an image of its natural obedience. The meaning varies according to the context: from execution agent to magistrate, but always a role of supervision.
H7860.portee: Understanding the role of the officer helps the reader grasp how God organizes a people: there is no direct command from the leader to the multitude, but a chain of responsible individuals who convey the will. For today's believer, it is a reminder that authority is a service, a relay of divine order; the officer does not give his own orders, but those he receives. It also shows that God, by giving a law to Israel, structures a people through clear roles and responsibilities.

sens: Officer of King David in charge of livestock
H7861.detail: Shithraï is a man who lived during the time of the divided kingdom and served King David. He was responsible for the oxen that grazed in Sharon, a fertile region of Palestine. The text in 1 Chronicles 27:29 mentions him among the officers that David had established to manage various aspects of his kingdom and resources.
H7861.origine: The name Shithraï means "my officers" in Hebrew. It comes from a root denoting administration and order. This name evokes his very function: to be one who organizes and commands on behalf of the king.
H7861.emploi: Shithraï appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:29. He is listed among the officers of King David, where each man is responsible for a category of royal goods: livestock, harvests, vineyards, etc. Shithraï is specifically in charge of the oxen grazing in Sharon. This mention shows the sophisticated administrative organization of David's kingdom and the importance given to managing the king's material resources.

sens: Valuable object brought as a sign of respect or homage
Voluntary gift presented to someone of higher status
Religious offering presented to God
H7862.detail:
1. The word shay denotes a material object of value — gold, clothing, or other goods — that is given to someone to show respect and deference. It is a concrete, visible gesture that accompanies the acknowledgment of authority. In Psalms 68:30, kings bring "gifts" to God, thus recognizing His sovereignty.
2. This gift is always voluntary and chosen, freely offered to the recipient, never imposed like a tax. It expresses the honor one bears and strengthens the relationship between the giver and the recipient. In Psalms 76:12, there is an invitation to "bring gifts" to the terrible God, a gesture where the generosity of the heart prevails.
3. When the recipient is God, the gift becomes a religious offering, that is, a form of worship and adoration. In Isaiah 18:7, the peoples bring "offerings" to the Lord of hosts on Mount Zion, thus acknowledging His cosmic sovereignty and holiness.
H7862.origine: The word shay comes from a Hebrew root evoking the idea of giving or presenting. Its fundamental meaning is that of a good transmitted voluntarily as a mark of honor or homage. It is related to other Hebrew terms designating gifts and offerings, but shay particularly emphasizes the gesture of respect and acknowledgment toward the recipient.
H7862.emploi: The word shay appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in solemn and religious contexts. Two occurrences are found in the Psalms (68 and 76), where it denotes the gifts that kings and nations bring to God in recognition of His reign and power. The third occurrence, in Isaiah 18, describes a prophetic vision where distant peoples bring offerings to the God of Israel on Mount Zion. In all cases, shay expresses an act of voluntary submission and homage to a higher authority — in this case, God Himself.
H7862.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that the relationship with God is also expressed through concrete and visible gestures of respect and deference. Offering a gift to God — whether material or spiritual (prayer, praise, obedience) — is to acknowledge His absolute sovereignty and our dependence on Him. The shay invites us not to separate inner faith from external and tangible worship.

sens: characteristic of what rises high
pride, arrogance
excessive pride
H7863.detail:
1. Height: the characteristic of what rises high, what elevates above all. It is primarily a physical image, that of remarkable altitude. In Job 20:6, the expression "his height would reach the heavens" speaks of the grandiose, eminent character of the dwelling of the wicked according to his own thought.
2. Pride: the word primarily designates the attitude of the heart that elevates itself, that judges itself superior to others. It is moral elevation turned into a flaw, the opposite of humility. This height of heart is that of the sinner who forgets God and exalts himself.
H7863.origine: The Hebrew word שִׂיא (si) comes from a root that evokes the idea of lifting up, rising high. The same family of roots produces words that speak of what ascends, dominates, or exalts. This spatial image — moving from low to high — naturally applies to pride: the proud "lifts himself" in his own esteem, he rises above others.
H7863.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 20:6, in a discourse where Zophar speaks of the wicked who claims that "his height would reach the heavens." It is a key moment: the text plays on irony — the wicked imagines that his personal elevation will be permanent and cosmic, while his ruin is imminent. The context shows that this "height" is not a commendable quality, but the expression of proud arrogance, of one who confuses his own brilliance with omnipotence.
H7863.portee: This word reminds the believer that pride — this temptation to elevate oneself, to believe that one rises above others or above God — is a destructive illusion. It invites true greatness: that of humility before God, as taught throughout Ecclesiastes and Proverbs. It is a lesson of humiliation before true glory.

sens: Another name for the mountain of Hermon
H7865.detail: 1. Zion is another name for the mountain of Hermon in the Holy Land. The Hebrew Bible uses this name to refer to the same majestic peak: in Deuteronomy 4:48, it specifies that the territory of Israel extended "to the mountain of Zion, which is Hermon," thus confirming the identity of the two names.
H7865.origine: The name Zion literally means "lofty" (elevated, high), which perfectly suits this majestic mountain. It is a variant of the name Hermon, though it is unclear why the two names coexist; some neighboring peoples of Israel used Zion while Hermon was the more common term in Hebrew. This is an example of the multiple names that important geographical locations could bear in antiquity.
H7865.emploi: Zion appears only once in the Bible in Deuteronomy 4:48, where Moses lists the borders of the Promised Land. This single mention is sufficient to establish it as a legitimate designation for Mount Hermon, the highest mountain visible from the Holy Land, which served as a major geographical landmark for delineating the territory of Israel to the north.

sens: city of the tribe of Issachar
H7866.detail: Shion is a city that belonged to the tribe of Issachar, located near Mount Tabor in northern Palestine. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, during the enumeration of the cities assigned to Issachar after the conquest of the land (Joshua 19:19).
H7866.origine: The name Shion likely means "ruin" in ancient Hebrew, perhaps suggesting that the site was known for this characteristic at the time the Israelites occupied it. Few historical or archaeological details are known about this locality.
H7866.emploi: Shion appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:19, as one of the cities in the territorial portion assigned to the tribe of Issachar after the conquest of Canaan. It is cited in an administrative list of borders and cities, without any particular narrative involving it.

sens: to become white or gray (referring to hair)
to age, to gain the experience of age
H7867.detail:
1. The word literally describes the fact that hair turns white or gray with age: it is a natural process visible on the head. Samuel says to Israel: "I am old, I have turned white," to show by this physical sign that his life has passed in service to God (1 Samuel 12:2).
2. By extension, the whitening of hair symbolizes old age and the wisdom gained over time. Job 15:10 speaks of "white hair" among the wise to denote those who have lived long and possess the experience of years.
H7867.origine: The Hebrew verb siv comes from a root that describes the color white or gray appearance. The word is related to the visible image of aging: hair losing its natural color. There is an equivalent Aramaic form (siv in Aramaic), showing that this term was understood in both main Semitic languages of the Bible.
H7867.emploi: The verb appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. Samuel uses it to assert his authority and legitimacy: after a long life in service to the people, his white hair testifies to his faithfulness and integrity (1 Samuel 12:2). In the book of Job, the term describes the wise with white hair, those who have the experience of past generations (Job 15:10). In both cases, to whiten is not merely a physical matter, but a visible sign of experience and moral authority.
H7867.portee: For the reader, this word reminds us that old age in the Bible is not a diminishment, but a visible testimony of God's grace and faithfulness through the years. White hair represents the wisdom gained and the honor of having lived long under divine protection. It is an invitation to respect those who have aged in serving God.

sens: aged person, with gray hair
chief or dignitary respected for his age and experience
member of a council of elders
H7868.detail:
1. The word primarily designates one whose hair has turned gray with age: it is the image of old age and the wear of time. In Hebrew, to be "gray" (siv) literally means to have white hair that marks the years lived.

2. By extension, the term applies to one who has the natural authority conferred by experience and age: an elder is a mature man deemed worthy of respect. Ezra 5:5 mentions "the elders of the Jews" whom the Persian governor allows to oversee the reconstruction of the Temple, acknowledging their weight in the community.

3. In the context of the return from exile (Ezra 5:9, 6:7, 6:8, 6:14), the elders form a council or delegation that speaks on behalf of the people, receives orders from the Persian kings, and supervises major works. It is an institutional function: the elders are the legitimate representatives of the Jewish community.
H7868.origine: The Hebrew root siv literally means "to be gray" or "to have white hair." It paints a natural image: hair that whitens with age. The noun "siv" (an elder) arises from this physical image, transposed into dignity: one who has gray hair is one who has lived, thus one who knows and should guide. This same root appears elsewhere in Hebrew to denote old age and the wisdom associated with it.
H7868.emploi: The word appears five times in the book of Ezra (chapters 5 and 6), all usages concerning the reconstruction of the Temple in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile (around 520 B.C.). In each occurrence, "elder" designates the Jewish leaders who interact with the Persian authority and supervise the works: in Ezra 5:5, the elders are questioned by the governor; in Ezra 5:9, they are asked about the authorization to build; in Ezra 6:7 and 6:8, King Darius orders that they be financially assisted for the construction; in Ezra 6:14, they successfully complete the Temple. The word remains stable: it always designates the same group of respected leaders.
H7868.portee: For today's believer, the word reminds us that experience and wisdom come with time and faithfulness. The elders of the return from exile embody transmission: they are men who survived captivity and know how to rebuild. The Bible values age here not as a burden, but as a resource of wisdom and moral authority. It is a call to respect those who have walked long with the Lord.

sens: The age of human life characterized by white and gray hair
The final stage of life, marked by bodily weakness
The accumulation of years that diminishes strength and sight
H7869.detail:
1. The word concretely refers to the advanced age of a person, recognizable by their white or gray hair — the visible sign of the passage of time. This is the basic image: the whiteness of hair is the symbol of old age. In 1 Kings 14:4, the prophet Ahijah has "fixed eyes due to old age": his sight has weakened because of his great age.
2. Beyond physical appearance, the word speaks of the exhaustion of strength. Old age is not just a matter of years: it is the time when the body refuses to function as before, when illness and fatigue take over. Ahijah is the perfect example — he can no longer see, paralyzed by his age.
3. Old age is also a period of dependence and vulnerability. The elderly person needs help, someone to move for them. Jeroboam's wife must go to Shiloh to consult Ahijah precisely because he cannot move: old age confines him.
H7869.origine: The Hebrew word שֵׂיב (sev) comes from a root that evokes whiteness and grayness — the image of hair turning white with age. It is a concrete noun: it primarily speaks of what is seen on the head of a very old person. Although rare in the Bible (only one occurrence in 1 Kings), it belongs to a family of words that revolve around old age and antiquity, reminding us that in the biblical mindset, age is a visible and respected reality.
H7869.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 14:4. It describes the prophet Ahijah, who has lost his sight due to his old age. Although rare, it is used to show that old age is not an abstract matter: it is a concrete reality that affects the body and its capabilities. The biblical context confirms it — old age is an inevitable stage of human life, often accompanied by weakness and fragility, but also by wisdom and spiritual experience.
H7869.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that human life has seasons, and that old age is one of them. It is not a punishment, but a reality that the Bible does not hide: the eyes weaken, the strength diminishes. Yet, the presence of Ahijah in the text shows that even in advanced old age, God can continue to speak through a man, and that age does not extinguish the prophetic role. It is an invitation to see old age not as an end, but as a stage where God's presence and wisdom can still be active.

sens: the state of being a prisoner, held against one's will
a group of prisoners, deportees
return to freedom after captivity
restoration, reinstatement to a previous state
H7870.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the state of captivity, the condition of the prisoner or deportee held in exile. In Psalms 126:1, it evokes the captives of Zion brought back to Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile: these people have left their land, constrained and forced, and now live as foreigners in a foreign land.
2. By extension, it can refer to the group of captives themselves, all those men, women, and children taken far from their homeland.
3. The word also carries the sense of the "return" of these captives: not only their physical return to their land but their restoration to a normal, familial, spiritual state. When "the Lord restored the captives of Zion," it is a redemption that is fulfilled.
4. More broadly, it encompasses the notion of restoration, reinstatement to a happier previous condition — being brought back from distress to freedom, from ruin to prosperity.
H7870.origine: The Hebrew word שִׁיבָה (shivah) comes from the root שׁוּב (shoub), which means "to turn," "to return." This root evokes the movement of one who turns back, who returns on their steps. In the context of the exiles, "bringing back the captives" is therefore not just about freeing prisoners: it is about making them return, bringing them back physically and spiritually to their starting point. The same root gives rise to verbs like "to repent" (to turn back to God) or "to turn away." It is a rich image: captivity is a distancing, and restoration is a return.
H7870.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalms 126:1, in the sole context of the restoration of Zion after the Babylonian exile. It is a key moment in Israel's history: the temple was destroyed, the population deported, and here, decades later, the Lord allows the survivors to return to the promised land. The context of Psalm 126 is a pilgrimage feast where the returning exiles sing their joy: "When the Lord restored the captives of Zion, we were like those who dream." It is a hymn of redemption and thanksgiving, where the word encapsulates the entire tragedy of exile and the grace of return.
H7870.portee: This word speaks to the Christian of God's restoring power. The exile to Babylon was not the end: the Lord brought back His people, He restored them. It is a promise: even in the captivity of sin or distress, God can bring us back to freedom and blessing. For the early Christians, read in the light of Jesus Christ, these verses about the return of Zion spoke of salvation and the restoration of all things by the Messiah.

sens: The act of remaining in a place for a limited time
The period during which one resides somewhere temporarily
H7871.detail:
1. The word refers to the act of staying, dwelling in a place, but in a temporary or provisional manner — not being established there permanently. In 2 Samuel 19:32, it refers to King David's stay at Mahanaim: this was not his usual residence, but a place where he had retreated for a given time (here, fleeing from his son Absalom). It is like when we talk today about someone's stay in the hospital or in a city while visiting.
2. The word can also emphasize the duration, the span of time during which one remains: "during his stay" means "the time he spent there." It is the momentary period of lodging and daily life in a place.
H7871.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root שׁוּב (choub), which means "to sit" or "to remain." The family includes words related to the idea of dwelling, residing, taking place in a location. It is a noun that expresses the action or state of one who stays: one settles there, lives there for a time.
H7871.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Samuel 19:32. It describes King David's stay at Mahanaim when he had to flee Jerusalem during Absalom's rebellion. Barzillai, a wealthy man from Gilead, supported and provided for him during this time. The context shows that the word applies to a forced or provisional stay, determined by events, not to a permanent settlement.
H7871.portee: This word speaks to us about the believer's status on earth: like David in flight, we are "strangers and pilgrims" (Hebrews 11:13). Our life here is but a stay, a temporary dwelling, for our true homeland is in heaven. It invites us not to become overly attached to the things of this world or the places of this world, but to keep our gaze toward our eternal home.

sens: White hair that marks advanced age
The state and period of life when one grows old
An old man, an elderly person
The dignity and wisdom associated with age
H7872.detail: 1. The word primarily refers to the white hair itself, the visible sign of aging. In Proverbs 16:31, "gray hair is a crown of glory," an image to show that gray hair, far from being a mark of decline, reflects a virtuous life. 2. It also signifies the time of old age, the ultimate period of existence. Genesis 15:15 promises Abraham that he will go "to your fathers" and be "buried at a good old age": this refers to all the time he has left to live before death. 3. The word can simply refer to an old man, an elderly person. Leviticus 19:32 commands: "You shall rise before the gray-headed and honor the aged," indicating that this term is used to speak of a person. 4. It also evokes honor and wisdom: in Proverbs 20:29, it is written that "the glory of young men is their strength, and the splendor of old men is their gray hair," suggesting that gray hair represents moral value and accumulated experience.
H7872.origine: The Hebrew word seyvah comes from a root meaning "to become gray" or "to whiten." The starting image is very concrete: it is the change of color of hair with age. In Hebrew, this word is related to terms that describe whiteness and discoloration. The Bible uses this word to speak of both the physical sign (gray hair) and the reality it represents (old age itself).
H7872.emploi: This word appears about 19 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the Torah, Proverbs, and Psalms. It is used very concretely: Genesis 44:29 speaks of Jacob's "gray hair" that will go down "with sorrow to the grave" if Benjamin does not return — it is an image of great tenderness, the aged father consumed by grief. In Leviticus 19:32, the law commands respect for the elderly, establishing that advanced age deserves honor. Proverbs uses the term to teach that gray hair, the fruit of a righteous life, is a glory (Proverbs 16:31). Psalm 71:18 asks God not to forsake the psalmist "until I am old and gray." The word oscillates between physical meaning and moral meaning: gray hair is not just a matter of appearance; it embodies the weight of experience and responsibility.
H7872.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to honor old age and those who experience it. Unlike cultures that despise advanced age, the Bible sees it as a richness: wisdom, experience, and the blessing of God. Understanding that "gray hair" is a "crown of glory" changes the perspective one has on elderly people and on one's own impending old age. It is a call to respect and cherish those who are nearing the end of their lives.

sens: to be occupied by a concern, a matter
to be in the process of reflecting or concentrating on something
H7873.detail:
1. The word refers to being absorbed, preoccupied with something: one is busy, one has their mind engaged elsewhere. When Elijah mocks the prophets of Baal at the time of the sacrifice (1 Kings 18:27), he ironically suggests that their god does not respond because he is "thinking" about something — that is, he is distracted, caught up in his own affairs, unable to hear the prophets' call.
2. More broadly, it is the idea of being in the process of reflecting or meditating, having one's mind occupied. Elijah's irony rests on this absurdity: a true God cannot be distracted like a man who is thinking about his affairs.
H7873.origine: The Hebrew word שִׂיג comes from a root expressing the idea of movement or diversion. The English gloss "pursuing" suggests an action of going toward something or moving away from it — thus "to think" in the sense of "to turn one's mind toward" something, to occupy oneself with it. It is a natural image in ancient languages: to think is primarily to direct one's attention.
H7873.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 18:27, in the mouth of Elijah mocking the prophets of Baal. It is part of an ironic enumeration of possible reasons why the god Baal does not react to the sacrifice: perhaps he is thinking about something, or he is busy elsewhere, or on a journey, or sleeping. It is a rare word, used to create a comic and derisive effect.
H7873.portee: This passage absurdly reminds us that the God of Israel is never distracted or absent, unlike idols and their false gods. Elijah's satire invites us to meditate on the vigilance and constant presence of the living God with His people.

sens: to cover with white lime
to apply a protective coating
to make visible or bright
H7874.detail:
1. To whitewash means to apply a layer of lime (a white powder obtained from limestone) on a surface, usually on stone or wood. This lime protects the stone from the elements and makes it shine. In Deuteronomy 27:2, the Israelites are commanded to set up large stones and whitewash them, which would make them visible from afar.
2. The action of whitewashing can also have a sense of revelation or clarity: to make something bright and pure. The whitewashed stones of Mount Ebal (Deuteronomy 27:4) would be visible and imposing witnesses of the Law written on them.
H7874.origine: The Hebrew verb שִׂיד (sid) refers to the action of painting or covering with lime. Its basic image is that of the bright whiteness of lime. This word remains infrequent in the Old Testament and belongs to the concrete vocabulary of construction techniques and the coating of buildings and structures.
H7874.emploi: The verb שִׂיד appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in Deuteronomy 27, when Moses commands Israel, upon entering Canaan, to set up whitewashed stones on Mount Ebal. These stones would serve as a memorial monument to inscribe the Law of the Lord. The usage is purely practical: it is about preserving and making visible these textual witnesses of the Covenant.
H7874.portee: This act of covering the stones with white lime symbolizes the desire to make the Law alive and bright in the eyes of all the people, as a lasting testimony that is inaccessible to forgetfulness. For the believer, this reminds us that the Word of God should be brought to the forefront, not hidden, and serve as a shining guide in each person's life.

sens: White powder obtained by burning bones or stone
White coating applied to stone for protection and whitening
Intense furnace, image of destruction
H7875.detail:
1. Lime is a white powder produced by calcining bones or limestone: it is a well-known construction and coating material in the ancient East. In Deuteronomy 27:2 and 27:4, Moses commands the Israelites to set up large stones and coat them with lime: this is to create a smooth, white surface on which to inscribe the Law, so that everyone can read it clearly.
2. When applied to stones, lime protects and brightens them: it is a protective coating and a means of solemnly marking an important place. This visible whiteness from afar symbolizes the clarity and publicity of the divine message.
3. In a prophetic image, Isaiah 33:12 speaks of "furnaces of lime," meaning intense fires where transformation occurs: it is no longer the useful material, but the trial by fire that consumes and destroys, comparing the peoples to burning thorns, consumed by judgment.
H7875.origine: The word שִׂיד (sid) comes from a root meaning "to burn" or "to calcine": it directly designates the product of this combustion. In Hebrew and in the languages of the ancient Near East, lime was well known as a durable construction material and was produced by calcining bones or limestone. The word reflects the very process by which it is obtained.
