H7875.emploi: The word appears 4 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Deuteronomy 27 where it refers to coating the stones of the covenant so that the Law can be inscribed legibly (two occurrences). A unique use in Isaiah 33:12 unfolds the image figuratively: no longer the useful material, but the destructive furnace, an image of divine judgment that consumes the enemies. Amos 2:1 completes the picture of the Near Eastern context. Each time, lime represents either a solemn and public marking or destruction by fire.
H7875.portee: Lime in Deuteronomy 27 reminds us that God's Law must not only be written but visible and accessible to all: it is not hidden but publicly proclaimed. In Isaiah 33, the image of fiery judgment warns us that those who oppose God will be consumed, while those who trust in God will be protected and restored.

sens: Set aside, cease to support or recognize
Voluntarily reject by turning elsewhere
Forget by no longer giving thought or affection
H7876.detail:
1. To abandon means to drop something or someone one was responsible for, to cease to support or uphold it. In Deuteronomy 32:18, Israel "abandoned" the Rock (God) who gave birth to them: a striking image of a break with the one who ensured their sustenance and very existence.
2. The verb also carries the idea of active rejection: turning away, deliberately turning one's back. It is not a mere distraction, but a deliberate act of separation.
3. Abandoning relates to forgetting, not as a lapse of memory, but as a refusal to recognize, cherish, or maintain the relationship — to forget "the God who gave you birth" (Deuteronomy 32:18) is to refuse to acknowledge Him as one's father and benefactor.
H7876.origine: The Hebrew root שׁיה expresses the idea of letting go, depriving oneself. It is rare in the Bible and concentrated in a few uses related to abandonment or rejection. The underlying image is that of a hand letting go, ceasing to hold.
H7876.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Deuteronomy 32:18, at the heart of the Song of Moses. There, Moses reproaches Israel for having "abandoned" the God who created and nourished them. The context is solemn and accusatory: Israel, in its ingratitude and unfaithfulness, has denied the one who gave them birth. This unique occurrence carries prophetic weight.
H7876.portee: This word reminds believers of the seriousness of unfaithfulness to God: to abandon God is not merely to err or weaken, it is an act of rejection and ingratitude towards the One who has given us existence and sustenance. It calls to conscience the loyalty owed to our Creator.

sens: Man from the divided monarchy period of Israel
H7877.detail: Schiza is a Reubenite, meaning a man from the tribe of Reuben. He is the father of Adina, one of the valiant warriors of King David. Schiza appears only once in the Bible, mentioned solely because his son Adina distinguished himself by his courage and loyalty in service to David (1 Chronicles 11:42).
H7877.origine: The name Schiza means "splendor" or "brightness" in Hebrew. It is a characteristic name from ancient Israel, formed from a root evoking brilliance and luminosity. This name may reflect the honor or dignity of the family, as his son would become one of David's renowned generals.
H7877.emploi: Schiza is mentioned only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 11:42. There he is presented as the father of Adina the Reubenite, leader of his tribe and one of the thirty elite warriors in the service of King David. His name is preserved only because his son excelled in the royal armies. No other biographical information is given about him in the Bible.

sens: Deeply reflect on something, turn it over in one's mind
Speak about something, talk about it aloud or to oneself
Sing or express through song
Complain, moan, sigh
H7878.detail:
1. To meditate means to think intensely and for a long time about a subject, to "ruminate" it in one's heart. It is particularly the act of reflecting on God's word, His promises, and His wonders: "I rise before the dawn and cry for help; I hope in your words" (Psalms 119:148). We meditate when we seek to understand, to internalize it.
2. To speak about something means to speak well of it or to bear witness, often publicly or to instruct others. In Psalms 105:2, we are invited to "speak of all His wonders." It is putting words to what we have discovered or understood.
3. To sing means to express joy or admiration through song, in music. In Judges 5:10, we are invited to "sing" the exploits of the Lord, blending voice with instrument.
4. To complain or moan means to express pain, worry, or distress. The psalmist says, "I moan" (Psalms 77:4), blending meditation with lamentation when the heart is troubled.
H7878.origine: This Hebrew root expresses the idea of "bringing forth" or "producing" a thought, sound, or word. It evokes the action of bringing something out of oneself: a deep reflection, a voice, a song, or a complaint. The family of the word includes "siakh" (bush, shrub), as the sound of the wind in the bushes recalls the murmur of one who meditates quietly or complains.
H7878.emploi: This verb appears about 20 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the Psalms and Wisdom literature (Job, Proverbs). It describes either the act of meditating on the Law and the works of God (Psalms 119 contains several uses), or that of speaking and bearing witness publicly (1 Chronicles 16:9: "Sing, sing in His honor"). It can also express the complaint or moaning of a troubled heart (Psalms 77:4). The context and the parallel with other verbs affect the nuance: near "singing," it means musical expression; near "moaning," the complaint; alone or with "ordinances," silent but intense meditation.
H7878.portee: This word reminds the believer that spiritual life is not reduced to a passive reading of the Word: it must be meditated upon, that is, turned over in the heart, ruminated, to truly know it. It also invites us to publicly testify to what we have discovered, to sing of God's wonders, and acknowledges that prayer can blend deep reflection with the expression of complaint or moaning in the face of difficulties.

sens: Expression of pain or dissatisfaction addressed to God or expressed before Him
Inner murmur, ruminating on one's troubles or concerns
Words expressing the turmoil or agitation of the soul
H7879.detail:
1. The complaint is primarily the expression of pain directed to God: it is the cry of the unfortunate who lays bare his sorrow, like the psalmist who "pours out his complaint before the Lord" (Psalms 102:1). Hannah, the mother of Samuel, also speaks of her excess of "pain and anguish," which has driven her to speak until now (1 Samuel 1:16).
2. It is also the inner rumination of one's pains: when Job says, "If I say: I want to forget my sufferings," he speaks of the sorrow that constantly occupies his mind (Job 9:27). It is this painful rumination, this endless return to his misfortunes, that the word designates.
3. More broadly, it is the word or expression that comes from this agitation of the soul: when someone speaks under the weight of anxiety, when he expresses his trouble or impatience (Psalms 55:3), his very words are a "complaint" in this sense.
H7879.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of stirring, moving, turning in every direction — a movement of body and spirit. In Hebrew, the same root also gives words to designate bushes or plants that sway in the wind, which clearly illustrates the image: something that is not still, that stirs. The biblical complaint is therefore this agitation of the soul seeking to express itself, this inner movement of pain.
H7879.emploi: The word appears about 14 times in the Hebrew Bible, notably in the Psalms and the book of Job. In the Psalms, it often refers to the complaint made to God: the psalmist asks the Lord to hear his complaint (Psalms 64:2, 102:1, 142:3). In Job, where the word is particularly frequent, it expresses painful rumination, the obsession with suffering: Job speaks of his complaints and his sorrow, always returning to his woes (Job 10:1, 23:2). The Segond translates this word as "complaint," "pain," "suffering," or "sorrow" depending on the context. The fundamental meaning remains the same: it is the expression or rumination of pain.
H7879.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that the Bible allows for complaint before God. Complaint is not a sin: it is a means of crying out to God in pain, as the psalmists and Job did. It also frees the reader from guilt when he experiences pain and does not know how to express it: the words "complaint" and "sorrow" show that the troubled soul can and must turn to God with its entire burden of pain.

sens: small woody plant with branches and leaves
wild vegetation of the desert and uncultivated lands
natural refuge or shelter for creatures
symbol of what is humble and ordinary
H7880.detail:
1. A shrub is a small woody plant, smaller than a tree, with branches and leaves: in the creation narrative, God had not yet caused these shrubs of the field to grow before it rained on the earth (Genesis 2:5).
2. In arid and desert lands, shrubs embody the sparse, wild, tough, and thorny vegetation: it is under such a bush that Hagar abandons her child in the desert of Beersheba (Genesis 21:15).
3. These plants offer a fragile refuge to miserable beasts and men: the unfortunate pull up weeds near the shrubs to feed themselves and hide, crying out under the bushes (Job 30:4, 30:7).
4. The shrub suggests the humble, the ordinary, that which grows without human care, in contrast to the great trees of the cultivated garden.
H7880.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of growing or sprouting. It is the basic, spontaneous plant that grows everywhere in dry soil without being sown. The Septuagint (an ancient Greek translation) often uses the word "thamnos" (bush) to translate it. It is a simple and concrete word, rooted in the observation of the nature of the ancient Near East.
H7880.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts of wild nature or distress. At the origins of the world (Genesis 2:5), it designates the vegetation that does not yet exist before creation. When Hagar flees to the desert (Genesis 21:15), a shrub becomes the only available shelter. In Job, in his complaints about human misery, the shrub is associated with extreme poverty: the unfortunate feed on roots near the bushes and hide there like beasts (Job 30:4, 30:7). The word always remains close to the ground, to what grows without cultivation, wild and accessible to all.
H7880.portee: The shrub reminds us that in times of distress or trial, even the most humble and ordinary creatures become essential. Hagar finds in a solitary bush in the desert the shelter that God provides for her. This word invites us to meditate on God's providence toward the weak: God does not despise the small, the wild, the insignificant. It is also an image of what grows naturally, without human effort, symbolizing free grace.

sens: Act of deeply reflecting, thinking about something attentively
Study, contemplation of a subject to understand it
Expression of a complaint, a concern entrusted to God
Feeling of reverential fear toward God
H7881.detail:
1. Meditation is the act of deeply reflecting, allowing one's mind to continually return to a thought or truth. This is why the psalmist says that the law of God is the object of his meditation all day long (Psalms 119:97): he thinks about it constantly, ruminates on it, savors it.
2. This word can also refer to the attentive study of a subject to know it better. He who meditates on God's precepts becomes more knowledgeable than his teachers, for the knowledge he gains comes directly from the heart (Psalms 119:99).
3. Meditation also includes the expression of our thoughts before God, including our complaints and worries. It is a form of inner prayer.
4. It is accompanied by a respectful fear: piety, that is, the fear of God that marks one who engages in spiritual reflection (Job 15:4).
H7881.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of speaking, murmuring, letting one's thoughts escape in a low voice. It is literally the murmur of the heart that meditates, like someone who ruminates on their thoughts within themselves. This image of murmuring reflects well the nature of meditation: an inner dialogue, almost inaudible, where the mind continually returns to the same truth or concern.
H7881.emploi: This word appears three times in biblical Hebrew. In Job 15:4, it designates piety, the fear of God that one who profanes the law destroys. In the two occurrences in Psalm 119 (verses 97 and 99), it is the constant object of the psalmist's thought: it is on the law and the precepts of God that he meditates day and night. These usages show that biblical meditation is not a vague daydream, but a sustained and respectful attention to the word of God, a spiritual practice that nourishes the soul and instructs the heart.
H7881.portee: Meditation invites the believer to go beyond the surface to delve deeper: not to be content with reading or hearing the word of God, but to continually return to it, turning it over in his heart to extract all its treasure. It is a practice of piety that gradually shapes the Christian character and replaces external agitation with inner listening.

sens: A hole dug in the ground, deep and narrow
A trap or ambush set against someone
Imminent danger or misfortune in which one risks falling
H7882.detail: 1. A pit is literally a hole dug in the ground, deep enough to cause someone to fall who does not see it. In Psalms 57:7, enemies "dig a pit" to make the psalmist fall — it is a concrete trap or an image of their malicious intent. 2. By extension, the word also refers to the trap itself, the cunning laid: "The proud dig pits before me" (Psalms 119:85) means that they prepare snares to make someone fall, literally or morally. 3. Figuratively, the pit also symbolizes danger, a fall, misfortune into which one risks sinking — which is why the psalmists ask God to preserve them from it.
H7882.origine: The Hebrew word שִׁיחָה (shichah) comes from a root that evokes the idea of digging or plowing. It properly designates what is dug: a pit, a hole, an excavation. The same root is found in other words related to worked earth or dug soil. In Hebrew, this word is often used to speak of traps or snares set by enemies.
H7882.emploi: The word appears twice in the Bible, both in the Psalms. In Psalms 57:7, it is the enemies who "dig a pit" under the psalmist's feet — an image of immediate danger and conspiracy against him. In Psalms 119:85, the proud "dig pits," which expresses how they lay traps to make him fall. In both cases, it is an image of the trap, the snare, an attempt to make someone fall into confusion or destruction.
H7882.portee: This word reminds the believer that the enemies of God and His people use cunning and conspiracy to make the faithful fall; but it also invites them to trust God for preservation. The pit is a real danger, but God is the one who sees the traps and frees those who rest in Him.

sens: river or canal marking the eastern border of Egypt
branch of the Nile or nourishing watercourse of Egypt
H7883G.detail:
1. The Schichor is a watercourse or canal that marks the boundary between Egypt and the land of Canaan. In Joshua 13:3, it is presented as the southwestern border of the region that the Israelites are to conquer: it is the starting point of a territorial description that goes north to Ekron and the land of the Philistines.
2. The Schichor is associated with the fertility and wealth of Egypt. In Isaiah 23:3, it is called the "Nile" and its waters allow for the harvest that enriches Egypt and makes it prosperous: it is a symbol of the economic and agricultural power of the country.
H7883G.origine: The Hebrew name "Schichor" literally means "black" or "dark," probably referring to the dark color of the silt-laden waters of the Nile during its floods. This watercourse is either the Nile itself in one of its branches or a canal connected to the Nile. The term reflects direct observation of water that stands out with its dark hue against the surrounding lands.
H7883G.emploi: The Schichor appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Joshua 13:3, it is mentioned as a geographical boundary, defining the western edge of the territory that God promises to the Israelites: this shows the importance of the word in the description of the Canaanite lands and their limits. In Isaiah 23:3, the same watercourse (called "Nile" there) is presented in a context of agricultural and commercial abundance, illustrating the prosperity of Egypt. These two uses emphasize that the Schichor was a major geographical reality, both a territorial boundary and a source of wealth.
H7883G.portee: For the biblical reader, the Schichor concretely marks the divine promise: it is a real, visible boundary that delineates the territory granted to the people of Israel. Mentioning this river by name anchors the narrative in verifiable geography and reminds us that God knows precisely the lands He gives.

sens: The Nile or a canal of the Nile, at the eastern border of Egypt
The southern boundary of the territory of Israel
H7883H.detail:
1. The Schichor is a river or canal related to the Egyptian Nile, located at the eastern border of Egypt. Its name means "black" in Hebrew, probably referring to the black waters of the Nile during its floods laden with silt. In Jeremiah 2:18, the prophet mentions "the waters of the Nile" to illustrate the folly of Israel turning to Egypt.
2. In the political and geographical context of Israel, the Schichor marks the southern limit of the conquered or claimed territory. In 1 Chronicles 13:5, it represents the southern boundary of the Israelite lands, and David gathers all the people "from the Schichor of Egypt to the entrance of Hamath" to signify the unity of the kingdom from south to north.
H7883H.origine: The Hebrew word שִׁיחוֹר (shichor) literally means "black." It is another designation for יְאֹר (yeor, the Nile), and derives its name from the color of the river's waters during its annual flooding. This name reflects the observation of the ancients of the visual characteristics of the Nile during its overflow, laden with dark alluvium.
H7883H.emploi: The word Schichor appears twice in the Bible translated into French. In 1 Chronicles 13:5, it precisely designates the southern boundary of the kingdom of Israel during David's time, serving as a major geographical landmark to delineate the extent of the territory. In Jeremiah 2:18, the same river (translated here as "Nile") symbolizes Egypt, the foreign power to which Israel turns inappropriately. Both uses show how this river, although Egyptian, becomes a fundamental reference for situating and understanding the political and spiritual issues of Israel.
H7883H.portee: The Schichor reminds the Christian reader that the earthly boundaries of God's people had a concrete reality and strategic importance. It also symbolizes the constant temptation of Israel to seek help and support from the powers of the world (Egypt) rather than trusting in God. This geographical detail invites reflection on the spiritual "boundaries" of the disciple: to what sources do we seek the water that refreshes?

sens: watercourse of the region of Asher
H7884.detail: A watercourse located in the Promised Land, in the territory of Asher, west of Mount Carmel (Joshua 19:26). The name literally means "blackness of whiteness," which probably describes the appearance of the watercourse or the landscape it traverses.
H7884.origine: The Hebrew name is composed of two elements: "Schichor" means "blackness" or "black," and "Libnath" means "whiteness" or "white." This combination of opposites (black and white) could evoke the variations in color of the watercourse depending on the season or light, or simply be a descriptive name of the place.
H7884.emploi: The name appears only once in the Bible, during the description of the boundaries of the territory assigned to the tribe of Asher (Joshua 19:26). It marks a western limit of this region, near Mount Carmel.

sens: oar with a flat blade at the end to propel a boat
action of rowing, propelling a vessel with oars
navigation and trade instrument
H7885.detail:
1. The oar is the stick equipped with a flat blade that is plunged into the water and pulled towards oneself to move a boat forward. It is the tool of the rower, a simple and ancient means of navigating rivers and seas. In Isaiah 33:21, the Lord promises Jerusalem a river so wide and magnificent that even oared vessels (the most common at the time) will not be able to cross it — so vast and inaccessible will the river be to enemies.
2. The oar also refers to the action of rowing itself, the patient work of the navigator who propels his boat. It is the image of movement, of effort to progress on the water.
3. By extension, the oar represents merchant and military ships, the activity of navigation that connects peoples and wealth. In the text of Isaiah, it symbolizes human power: the oars are what enemy powers would use to attack Jerusalem, but they will never penetrate it.
H7885.origine: The Hebrew word שַׁיִט comes from a root that evokes movement in water and gliding. It designates the concrete instrument used since the earliest antiquity for navigation. In the Bible, this word is rare and mainly appears to describe the oars of merchant and military ships, symbols of ancient navigation and trade.
H7885.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 33:21. It specifically refers to the oars of merchant ships which, according to the prophet, will not be able to cross the wonderful river that the Lord will grant to Jerusalem in restoration. It is a technical and concrete word, used to describe the maritime reality and naval power.
H7885.portee: This word reminds us that the apparent power of men — even that of their ships and oars — is limited. The Lord alone can transform a river into an impenetrable barrier. For the believer, it is an invitation to trust in God rather than in human defenses: His protection surpasses any military strategy.

sens: He who is to come, announced in the blessing of Judah
H7886.detail: 1. Schilo is a mysterious figure mentioned only once in the blessing that Jacob pronounces on his son Judah in Genesis 49:10. The word literally means "he who comes" or "he to whom it belongs" — a person whose arrival will mark the end of Judah's power and the obedience of the peoples. It is a veiled messianic promise: Jacob prophesies that the scepter (royal power) will remain with Judah until the arrival of this figure, who will bring the submission of the nations.
H7886.origine: The Hebrew word שִׁילֹה (shiloh) has a debated meaning. Some link it to a root meaning "he who sends" or "he who rests," but the precise etymology remains uncertain. Some scholars have seen it as a proper name — the city of Shiloh — or a play on words regarding the streets of Jerusalem ("his streets"). In the history of the Church, this word has been widely understood as a prophecy of the coming Messiah.
H7886.emploi: Schilo appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 49:10, in the solemn context of Jacob's final blessing to his twelve sons before his death. This verse is one of the oldest messianic prophecies in the Old Testament. Ancient Jews and early Christians interpreted it as announcing the arrival of a king or deliverer who would bring universal peace and the obedience of the nations. The uniqueness of this mention and the mystery surrounding it make it one of the most enigmatic prophetic words in the sacred text.
H7886.portee: This prophecy of Schilo teaches that the history of Israel is oriented towards a future hope — the arrival of a figure who will calm the peoples and establish his authority. For Christians, this word sheds ancient light on Jesus Christ, showing how God wove the announcement of the Messiah into the patriarchal blessings. It invites us to see that even the most obscure passages of Scripture carry prophetic depth that is revealed in the light of the Cross and the Resurrection.

sens: city of Canaan in Ephraim
seat of the sanctuary and the Ark of the Covenant
religious center and pilgrimage site of the people of Israel
symbol of rest and divine presence in Israel
H7887.detail:
1. Shiloh is a city in Canaan located in the territory of the Ephraimites, north of Bethel, on an important route to Shechem (Judges 21:19). It is identifiable by its precise geographical position: it is a well-known place where a great festival of the Lord takes place every year.

2. After the conquest of the Promised Land, Shiloh becomes the seat of Israel's sanctuary: it is there that the Ark of the Covenant and the Tent of Meeting (the Tabernacle) find their stable place (Joshua 18:1). It is the spiritual heart of the nation, where the visible presence of God resides.

3. Shiloh is the place where Samuel grew up after being offered by his mother Hannah, under the guidance of the priest Eli (1 Samuel 1:24, 3:21). Crowds of pilgrims come there every year to worship and present sacrifices to the Lord (1 Samuel 1:3).

4. Despite this central function, Shiloh is abandoned by God because of the wickedness of the people (Jeremiah 7:12). The prophet cites it as a warning: the Lord treated this holy place as He will treat the Temple of Jerusalem if the people persist in unfaithfulness. The very name of Shiloh evokes rest in the divine presence, a rest that sin ultimately destroys.
H7887.origine: The name Shiloh (Hebrew שִׁלוֹ) literally means "the place of rest" (from the root שׁלה, "to be at peace"). It expresses the idea that this place is intended to be a stable resting place for the Ark and the sanctuary of God's people. After years of pilgrimage in the desert, Shiloh represents the definitive establishment of the divine dwelling among Israel, even though this stability will later be replaced by Jerusalem.
H7887.emploi: Shiloh appears about 30 times in the Bible, mainly in the book of Joshua (where it becomes the seat of the sanctuary), in Judges (for pilgrimages and religious festivals), in the first book of Samuel (associated with the prophet Samuel and the priest Eli), and in Jeremiah (where the prophet invokes it as an example of divine judgment). Throughout the biblical narrative, Shiloh transitions from a flourishing religious center and place of divine presence (the time of Joshua and Samuel) to a deserted and destroyed city, symbolizing what happens when the people abandon the Lord (Jeremiah 7:12). The context changes: initially, it is a place of order, assembly, and legitimate worship; later, it becomes a place of spiritual decay.
H7887.portee: Shiloh teaches Christians that the visible presence of God among His people is never a guarantee against judgment if faithfulness disappears. Rest in the house of God relies on obedience and fear of the Lord. For the believer today, this ancient city reminds us that privilege and spiritual stability require a constant response of faith and repentance.

sens: City of Israel located in the region of Ephraim
Inhabitant of Shiloh
Relating to Shiloh or its inhabitants
H7888.detail: 1. Shiloh is a city in Israel in the Promised Land, where the tabernacle and the ark of the covenant were placed after the conquest (Joshua 18:1). Its name means "place of rest." 2. A Shilonite is a man or woman born in Shiloh or originating from this city, like Asaiah mentioned in 1 Chronicles 9:5. 3. The adjective "of Shiloh" qualifies what belongs to Shiloh or comes from there: it is notably applied to the prophet Ahijah, who was from Shiloh and announced to Jeroboam the division of the kingdom (1 Kings 11:29, 1 Kings 12:15).
H7888.origine: The name Shiloh (שִׁלוֹ in Hebrew) literally means "place of rest" or "tranquility." It was a holy place in Israel, where God commanded the tabernacle to be placed during the settlement in the Promised Land. The term "Shiloh" or "Shilonite" thus designates both a specific geographical location and the people who lived there.
H7888.emploi: The word appears six times in the Old Testament. Five times, it qualifies the prophet Ahijah ("Ahijah of Shiloh"), whose prophecies regarding the division of Solomon's kingdom are mentioned several times: in 1 Kings 11:29, King Jeroboam meets him; in 1 Kings 12:15 and 2 Chronicles 10:15, his word is confirmed; in 1 Kings 15:29 and 2 Chronicles 9:29, his words are fulfilled. Once (1 Chronicles 9:5), the word directly designates the inhabitants of Shiloh: the Shilonites.
H7888.portee: Ahijah of Shiloh embodies the prophet faithful to God, whose word is fulfilled with certainty. His prophecies mark a major turning point in the history of Israel: the division of the kingdom under Jeroboam. For the reader, this name reminds us that God speaks to His people through His servant prophets and that His word will never fail, even in the midst of political crises.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy
H7889.detail: Simon is a Judean mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:20. He is the father of four sons: Amnon, Rinnah, Ben-Hanan, and Thilon. Nothing else is known about him other than this genealogy, recorded in the archives of the tribe of Judah to preserve the memory of the families of God's people.
H7889.origine: The name Simon comes from Hebrew and means "desert." It is a name that may evoke the harshness of the desert or perhaps a connection to the arid regions of Judah. Men bearing this name also appear in the New Testament (notably the apostle Simon Peter), but this Shimon from 1 Chronicles is a distinct character.
H7889.emploi: Simon appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:20, in a genealogy of the tribe of Judah established during the time of the divided monarchy (after the separation between Israel and Judah). His role is limited to being mentioned as the father of four sons, testifying to his place in the genealogical history of Israel.

sens: Produce a melody with the voice, alone or in a group
Praise God or celebrate His works through song
Celebrate an event or a victory by singing
Exercise the profession of singer-musician in the service of worship
Resound, make a voice or musical sound heard
H7891.detail:
1. To sing is to produce a melody with one's voice: it is the simple and universal action of forming musical notes. Moses and the children of Israel "sang" this song to the Lord after crossing the Red Sea (Exodus 15:1), leading the words with their voices.
2. Singing becomes praising God or celebrating His wonderful acts: the voice carries recognition and joy. The psalmist cries, "I will sing of mercy and justice" (Psalms 101:1), putting into sound the perfections of God.
3. Singing can also mark a victory or an important event, a cry of collective joy. Deborah and Barak sing after their victory in battle (Judges 5:1).
4. The word also designates one who sings by profession, notably in the Temple worship: the "singers" and "singer-women" (Ezra 2:65), official musicians who served God through their art, like the Levitical singers in 1 Chronicles 15:27.
5. Finally, to sing can mean to resound or echo: the voice that rises and spreads, the melodious effect that fills a place.
H7891.origine: The verb שִׁיר (shir) expresses the idea of making sound resonate, modulating the voice. The root evokes the sound that rises and carries. This root has given rise to the noun שִׁיר (shir, "song" or "chant"), and it is from here that the Greek word ᾠδή (ôdê, "song") comes, which is found in the New Testament. The basic image is that of a voice that rises melodiously, carried by joy or devotion.
H7891.emploi: The verb "to sing" appears 79 times in the Hebrew text of the Bible. It is a word found in all poetic and historical books: very frequent in the Psalms (where the psalmist sings his praises and fears), present in historical narratives (the victory of Deborah, that of David) and in the books of Chronicles (where the singers play an official role in the Temple worship). The meaning varies slightly: sometimes to sing is simply to vocalize ("I will sing to the Lord"), sometimes it is to celebrate or glorify ("I will sing of mercy"), sometimes it is to be the professional musician in charge of worship. In the Psalms, it is the act of praying and praising through melody; in Chronicles, it is an organized liturgical ministry. Everywhere, singing is an act that unites human joy and recognition towards God.
H7891.portee: Singing reveals that the praise of God is not limited to words: it engages the whole body, the voice, emotion, and music. The Bible shows that singing is a profound act of faith, a way to transform joy or even suffering into worship. For the Christian, this word reminds us that we are invited not only to believe and pray in silence but also to express our faith through communal and personal singing, which honors God and strengthens the heart.

sens: Musical expression with lyrics that is sung
Religious song or praise offered to God
Hymn of the Levitical choirs in the temple
Melody or musical composition in general
Sung word, capable of touching the heart
Ironical use to designate a vain or pleasant but hollow word
H7892A.detail:
1. The chant is primarily a concrete musical act: someone produces a melody with their voice, often accompanied by instruments (tambourine, harp, trumpets). In Genesis 31:27, Laban would have wanted to send Jacob away "in the midst of rejoicing and songs, with the sound of the tambourine and the harp": the songs are the festive musical expressions that punctuate a celebration.
2. In Israelite worship, the chant becomes religious and liturgical: it is a privileged form of praise or prayer addressed to God. Many psalms bear the heading "Song" (Psalms 46:1, 92:1, 128:1), marking that they are intended to be sung during worship.
3. The chant of the Levites is a sacred function in the temple: in 1 Chronicles 6:31-32 and 2 Chronicles 29:27, musicians sing during sacrifices, guiding the collective prayer of the people.
4. As a composition, the word designates a complete musical work: Solomon "composed three thousand songs" (1 Kings 4:32), showing that one can have several distinct and memorable songs.
5. The chant touches the soul: the psalmist says, "You have put a new song in my heart" (Psalms 40:4), suggesting that singing is also the expression of what one feels deeply.
6. In contrast, the chant of fools is vain: "Better to hear the rebuke of the wise than to hear the song of fools" (Ecclesiastes 7:5), for the sung word can be seductive without being true.
H7892A.origine: The Hebrew word שִׁיר (shir) comes from a root that evokes the action of producing a melody. Its synonyms or related words include שִׁירָה (shirah, "song" or "poetry"). Throughout the biblical Hebrew literature, the word refers to a full experience: music, word, and emotion together. It is a word fundamentally linked to the cultic and communal life of Israel.
H7892A.emploi: The word שִׁיר appears about 76 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is largely concentrated in the Psalms (over 40 occurrences, often in titles or headings), where it qualifies hymns intended for worship. It is also found in Chronicles, reflecting the organization of the temple's musical service (1 Chronicles 6, 13, 15, 25; 2 Chronicles 5, 7, 23, 29). Outside of the liturgical context, the word applies to any musical composition (1 Kings 4:32) or songs of rejoicing (Genesis 31:27). In the Prophets, the chant sometimes becomes a symbol of life and joy (Isaiah 26:1) or, conversely, of vanity (Amos 5:23, 6:5, 8:10). Ecclesiastes uses it to explore the fragility of earthly pleasures.
H7892A.portee: For the Christian reader, the chant reveals that God delights in the musical expression of faith. The Psalms show that singing is not a religious luxury, but a legitimate means of praying, praising, and memorizing the truth. It is also a call: if the song of fools can seduce, the song of the heart renewed in Christ must testify to a true conversion.

sens: Poetic composition intended to be sung
Hymn or sacred poem
Lyrical testimony of praise or reproach
H7892B.detail:
1. The cantique is primarily a poetic composition accompanied by music, made to be sung: this is why Moses "wrote this cantique" and taught it to the children of Israel (Deuteronomy 31:22), so that they would remember it and recite it together.
2. It is a solemn hymn that celebrates or proclaims a spiritual reality: the cantique of Exodus 15:1 sings the miracle of crossing the Red Sea — "I will sing to the Lord, for He has triumphed gloriously" — and that of Numbers 21:17 praises the coming of the miraculous water from the well.
3. The cantique can also be a testimony that passes to posterity: God commands Moses to write a cantique "that shall serve as a witness against the children of Israel" (Deuteronomy 31:19), a living proof of divine commitments and the people's unfaithfulness, preserved in the mouths and memories.
H7892B.origine: The Hebrew word שִׁירָה (shirah) comes from the root שׁיר (shir), which means "to sing." This root evokes the very sound of the voice that rises in melody. The word naturally designates the product of singing: the composition, the text, and the music that go together. Words from the same family appear throughout the Bible to designate song, singers, and songs.
H7892B.emploi: The word "cantique" appears eleven times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in a solemn and liturgical context. The first three occurrences (Exodus 15:1, Numbers 21:17, Deuteronomy 31:19-22) concern major cantiques: that of deliverance at the Red Sea, that of the miraculous spring, and that which Moses composes as an act of covenant. Moses "pronounces" it before the entire assembly (Deuteronomy 31:30). Other cantiques celebrate events or heartfelt calls: the cantique of David after his deliverances (2 Samuel 22:1, Psalms 18:1), that of Isaiah on God's beloved vineyard (Isaiah 5:1). Each cantique is an embodied act of faith, intended to be passed down from generation to generation.
H7892B.portee: The cantique teaches the believing reader that praise, prayer, and testimony must be preserved in a memorable and transmissible form: they are not fleeting feelings, but truths that one meditates on, sings, and repeats. Throughout the Bible, the cantiques are the traces that God Himself leaves in the hearts of His people, acts of memory that give weight to faith. This is why the Christian church has always sung to keep its hope and its covenant with God alive.

sens: White or translucent stone, very fine and smooth, used for ornaments and luxury objects
H7893.detail: 1. Alabaster is a natural stone, white or slightly translucent, very compact and easy to polish. It is prized for its delicate beauty and fine grain. In the passage of 1 Chronicles 29:2, King David lists the precious materials he has gathered for the construction of the Temple: he mentions white alabaster among the shining stones and precious stones, alongside gold, silver, and marble. It is a material of great value, reserved for the most prestigious constructions and objects.
H7893.origine: The Hebrew word shaïsh designates alabaster, a fine white limestone. In Egypt and Mesopotamia, this stone was highly valued for vases, statuettes, and temple ornaments. The word reflects the cultural importance of this material in the ancient Near East: it was one of the noblest materials that a king could dedicate to the sanctuary of his God.
H7893.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 1 Chronicles 29:2. David lists the materials he has assembled for Solomon to build the Temple: gold, silver, bronze, iron, precious wood, precious stones. White alabaster appears in this list as one of the most refined and costly materials, underscoring the extraordinary nature of the royal endowment intended for the house of God.
H7893.portee: This word reminds us that the Old Testament values beauty and material excellence when they are consecrated to the worship of God. Precious stones and white alabaster symbolize the seriousness and generosity with which we should honor the Lord. It is a call not to remain poor in our offering to God, but to give what we have of the best.

sens: High-ranking officer at the royal court, secretary or scribe of King Solomon
H7894.detail: 1. Schischa is a character who holds an important administrative position in the palace of King Solomon: he is the father of two sons, Elihoreph and Achijah, who themselves serve as royal secretaries (1 Kings 4:3). This position of royal secretary was one of the most prestigious in the Israelite monarchy, responsible for official documents and royal correspondence.
H7894.origine: The name Schischa literally means "the Eternal contends" (or "the Eternal disputes"), formed from two Hebrew elements. It refers to the same person designated by several slightly different names according to the texts: Schischa in 1 Kings 4:3, Shavsha in 1 Chronicles 18:16, and Sheva in 2 Samuel 20:25. This variation of names is common in ancient biblical texts. Some commentators relate it to the name Seraja (Seraiah).
H7894.emploi: Schischa appears in the lists of high officials of the united kingdom of Israel. He is mentioned as the father of the two royal secretaries Elihoreph and Achijah during Solomon's reign (1 Kings 4:3). According to other parallel passages, he may have also served under King David in the same administrative role. His name is listed among the important officers of the court, alongside the archivist Jehoshaphat and other dignitaries of the kingdom.

sens: King of Egypt who reigned during the reigns of Solomon and Rehoboam
Pharaoh who welcomed Jeroboam in exile
Egyptian sovereign who attacked Jerusalem and plundered the temple
H7895.detail: Schischak is the name of an Egyptian pharaoh who played an important role in the political history of Israel during the time of the divided kingdom. He first offered asylum to Jeroboam, who was fleeing from Solomon's persecution (1 Kings 11:40), which shows the Egyptian influence in the internal affairs of the united kingdom. Then, in the fifth year of Rehoboam's reign, he launched a military expedition against Jerusalem (1 Kings 14:25; 2 Chronicles 12:2), likely to establish his dominance over the southern regions of the Levant. According to the account in 2 Chronicles, this invasion occurred because Israel had sinned against the Lord (2 Chronicles 12:2), illustrating the biblical theology of divine judgment. During his attack, Schischak systematically plundered the treasures of the temple and the royal palace, including the precious gold shields that Solomon had made (2 Chronicles 12:9). However, the Lord intervened on behalf of Judah: when the king and the leaders repented, God refused to completely destroy them and limited the calamity (2 Chronicles 12:5-7). Historically, Schischak corresponds to the Egyptian pharaoh Sheshonk I, the first king of the 22nd dynasty, whose inscriptions in Egypt confirm a military campaign in Syria-Palestine.
H7895.origine: The Hebrew name שִׁישַׁק (Schischak) etymologically means "greedy for fine linen" (according to the English gloss), although this etymology remains debated among scholars. The word is borrowed or has correspondences with Egyptian names. It historically designates the pharaoh known in Egyptology as Sheshonk I, founder of the 22nd Bubastite dynasty, who reigned in Egypt during the 10th century BC.
H7895.emploi: Schischak appears six times in the Bible, always in the books of Kings and Chronicles, reflecting his importance for the history of the divided monarchy. He is first presented as a political ally welcoming Jeroboam in exile (1 Kings 11:40). Then he becomes the instrument of divine judgment against the kingdom of Judah under Rehoboam. The two books of Chronicles further develop the narrative: they emphasize that this invasion was a consequence of national sin, but also on the divine grace that limited destruction after the repentance of the king and the leaders. Schischak's attack marks a historical turning point: it economically weakened Judah after the height of Solomon's reign and established temporary Egyptian predominance over the Levantine kingdoms.
H7895.portee: The story of Schischak teaches that even the great political powers of the world act according to God's plans. His invasion illustrates the biblical principle that national sin attracts divine judgment, but it also shows that sincere repentance provokes a merciful intervention from the Lord. For the believer, this account reminds us that political and military events are not the result of chance, but that God governs them to call his people to conversion and trust in his sovereignty.

sens: to place, put something in a location
to arrange, organize in order
to establish, constitute, appoint to a position
to direct, turn towards a goal
to reduce to nothing, devastate
to impose, load onto
H7896G.detail:
1. To physically place: to put or set something somewhere. Jacob "put together" the striped and black lambs to separate them from Laban's flock (Genesis 30:40). This is the concrete act of placing or arranging.

2. To arrange, organize in order: to organize several things according to a plan. The horsemen "arrange themselves for battle" at the gates (Isaiah 22:7) — they arrange themselves in military order.

3. To establish, constitute, appoint: to install someone in a charge or position. The king's children "will be established as princes throughout the land" (Psalms 45:17) — this is placing them in a position of dignity.

4. To direct, turn towards: to orient attention or face in a direction. Balaam "turned his face towards the desert" (Numbers 24:1) — he refocused his attention.

5. To reduce, devastate: to annihilate or ruin. The land is "besieged" (Psalms 3:7) — put in a state of siege, pressed from all sides.

6. To impose, load onto: to place a weight, a burden, or a judgment on someone. This is to weigh something upon a person.
H7896G.origine: The Hebrew verb שִׁית (shit) primarily means "to place, to put." It comes from a root that expresses the action of putting something in place. The word belongs to a rich family: it has produced names like שִׁיתָה (the placing, the structure). In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), this verb often translates the Greek τίθημι (tithèmi), which carries the same fundamental meaning of placing or establishing. The image is that of something being placed, set in place with intention.
H7896G.emploi: This verb appears 47 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms (28 times), as well as in the major prophetic and historical books. It denotes both a very concrete act — placing a hand, arranging flocks — and a more abstract act: establishing a king or a promise (Psalms 45:17: the children "will be established as princes"), or directing attention (Numbers 24:1). The verb can also express a negative action: to destroy or reduce to ruin (Isaiah 5:6: the vineyard becomes desolation). In the Psalms of request, it often describes the action of the enemy who besieges or surrounds (Psalms 3:7). The Segond translates this term as "to do," "to put," "to establish," or "to impose" depending on the context.
H7896G.portee: This word reminds us that God acts with intention: he "places" events, people, and kingdoms according to his plan. When we see that enemies "besiege" (Psalms 3:7), we understand that it is a concrete reality — but God remains the one who "establishes" princes and holds history in his hands. For the believer, this verb also evokes the idea that our life is not a disorder: God "places" our steps, and we are called to put our trust in him.

sens: To place, to put something physically
To entrust, to hand over a burden or responsibility to someone
To establish, to institute, to fix something in a lasting way
To apply or direct towards a particular goal
To impose, to inflict a condition or penalty
H7896H.detail: 1. To place or put something concretely: to put a hand on someone or something, to deposit it somewhere. It is the simple act of changing the position or place of an object (Genesis 48:14: Israel "laid" his hands on the heads of his grandsons). 2. To entrust or hand over a responsibility to someone, assigning them a task. It is to give a moral or practical burden (Ruth 4:16: the woman "took" the child to raise him, she welcomed him into her care). 3. To establish or institute something permanent or essential. It is to fix a new reality, a law or an order that persists (Genesis 3:15: God "will put" enmity between the serpent and the woman — He establishes a lasting hostility). 4. To direct or fix the mind, heart, or a mental capacity towards something. It is to place intention or wisdom in someone (Job 38:36: "Who has put wisdom in the heart?"). 5. To impose or burden someone with a condition, often painful or constraining. It is to weigh something on someone (Job 9:33: an arbiter who "puts" his hand on us both to judge us together).
H7896H.origine: The Hebrew root שׁית expresses the fundamental idea of placing, putting in place, or fixing. It often appears in contexts where it is about laying down, establishing, or founding something. The word can also mean to destroy or devastate (as in "to lay waste"). It is a very common verb in the Old Testament to express the action of placing, instituting, or imposing.
H7896H.emploi: This verb appears 21 times in the provided passages, primarily in Genesis, the book of Job, and the Psalms. It denotes both a concrete physical gesture (placing a hand, depositing a child) and a legal or spiritual action (establishing a covenant, setting aside, imposing a condition). In the passages from Genesis, it often concerns intentional and significant gestures (Israel's hand intentionally placed on Ephraim's head). In Job and the Psalms, it often takes on a more abstract or metaphorical hue: putting wisdom in the heart, putting someone in charge of overseeing something. The word can also express the establishment of a new or definitive reality, as when God "puts" enmity between the serpent and the woman — He establishes a lasting order.
H7896H.portee: This verb helps the Christian reader understand how the Bible speaks of divine and human action in concrete and intentional terms. When God "puts" something (wisdom in the heart, enmity, etc.), it is a decisive action that establishes a new reality. This shows that the Lord acts with intention and authority. For the believer, it is a call to recognize that God places, establishes, and institutes according to His will — nothing is left to chance.

sens: To place something or someone somewhere
To establish, to institute, to assign a role or function
To set a term, a limit, a specific moment
To strike, to reach someone in a devastating way
To prepare, to make ready
H7896I.detail:
1. To put means to place or set something: it is the concrete action of depositing, installing. Genesis 4:25 uses it in the sense of giving birth ("God has given me another son"), where putting to birth is equivalent to "placing" a child among the living.
2. To establish or institute means to assign someone a place, a rank, a mission: to make someone something, to constitute them in a role. This meaning is found in passages where a fate or judgment is fixed.
3. To set a term or limit means to draw a definitive boundary that nothing can exceed. Job 38:11 illustrates this: God says to the sea, "you shall not go beyond," you will stop at this precise point that I have marked.
4. To strike with dread or terror: it is a blow that reaches and paralyzes. Psalms 9:21 asks God to strike the enemies with fear, reducing them to silence.
5. To prepare means to arrange in advance, to put in order for a future moment. Hosea 6:11 speaks of a harvest prepared, ready to be reaped at the appointed time.
H7896I.origine: The Hebrew verb שׁית (shit) comes from a root that fundamentally means "to place" or "to put." It is a very ancient and common verb in biblical Hebrew, used to describe the simple action of putting something in a place, then extended to figurative meanings: to establish, to institute, to determine. The root evokes the primary image of the physical gesture that founds everything: to place something in a stable and intentional way.
H7896I.emploi: This verb appears 5 times in the provided usages, spread across Genesis, Job, Psalms, and Hosea. Each occurrence shows a different nuance of the verb: first the act of giving birth (Genesis), then the fixing of an imposing limit (Job 38), the determination of a term (Job 14), the action of striking or imposing (Psalms), and the preparation of a judgment (Hosea). The verb always retains the idea of a firm and decisive action: the one who puts something establishes something that remains, that imposes itself, that counts.
H7896I.portee: Understanding this verb helps the reader grasp how God acts in the Old Testament: not in a vague or hesitant manner, but by placing, establishing, fixing. When God puts a limit or prepares a harvest, it is a sovereign and irrevocable act. It also sheds light on human responsibility: to put something in place is to assume it, to fix it in reality. For the Christian, this word reminds us that God leaves nothing to chance: He places, establishes, prepares with authority.

sens: A burden or load imposed on someone
Responsibility for a fault or sin
Punishment or judgment that results from it
H7896J.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes a weight, a burden imposed on someone — like placing an object on their shoulders. In Numbers 12:11, Aaron begs Moses: "Do not let us bear the burden of sin"; he speaks of the crushing weight of guilt that God has placed on him and Miriam.
2. This burden is linked to the responsibility for a fault: it is the serious consequence of a wrongful act. Here, Miriam and Aaron have spoken against Moses, and they feel that God has struck them because of this sin.
3. By extension, the burden became the punishment or divine judgment itself — no longer just the weight of guilt, but the suffering or punishment that follows.
H7896J.origine: The Hebrew verb שִׁית (shit) fundamentally means "to put" or "to place" — the image of a hand that places something somewhere. In the context of faults and sin, this meaning has specialized: to put a burden on someone is to impose a charge, to assign them a responsibility. The word refers to the act of fixing or establishing something firmly and definitively.
H7896J.emploi: This verb appears only once in the French translation of the Bible (Numbers 12:11), where it is rendered as "burden." This unique usage shows Aaron pleading with Moses to intercede with God so that the consequence of sin (Miriam's illness) may be lifted. The usage reveals how the Hebrews conceived of sin: not as an internal stain to be erased, but as an objective burden that God places on the guilty. Aaron asks that this weight be removed.
H7896J.portee: This word reminds the reader that sin is never a light or personal matter: it is a burden that imposes itself, an objective reality that God judges and for which He holds humans accountable. But it also shows that this burden can be lifted through intercession and grace — Aaron dares to ask Moses to intervene, and God responds to the prayer. It is a lesson in responsibility and hope.

sens: To place one's attention, heart on something
To consider attentively, examine
To notice, observe
To give importance to, to be concerned about
H7896K.detail:
1. Taking to heart means to set one's mind and attention on something, to fix it in one's heart as a concern: when Pharaoh "did not take to heart" the plagues (Exodus 7:23), he refuses to let these events affect his decision. It is the opposite of indifference.
2. To observe means to examine something attentively to truly know it: in Psalms 48:14, we are called to "observe" the city's ramparts so that we can recount them to the next generation, as if we want to study them thoroughly.
3. To draw instruction means to notice something and learn a lesson from it: the one who says "I have drawn instruction" (Proverbs 24:32) has looked at the laziness of the lazy and has gleaned useful wisdom for his own conduct.
4. To take heed to the road (Jeremiah 31:21) means to pay attention to the path, to consciously notice it so as not to be misled — an invitation to practical vigilance.
H7896K.origine: This Hebrew root expresses the action of placing, setting, or establishing something. From this concrete sense of "to place" or "to fix," the word develops the figurative meaning of "to fix one's mind on," "to pay attention to." It is a movement from physical action to mental intention: one places something in one's heart as one places an object on a table.
H7896K.emploi: This verb appears seven times in the provided biblical usages, mostly in a context of attention or concern of the heart. With complements like "to heart," it expresses the emotional or mental reaction to an event: Pharaoh ignores the plagues, Absalom invites his sister not to worry, Tamar suffers. Without this complement, the verb retains varied nuances: to observe a place (Psalms 48:14), to draw a lesson (Proverbs 24:32), or to pay attention to a road (Jeremiah 31:21). The common idea is always one of emphasis, of fixing the mind.
H7896K.portee: For the Christian reader, this word invites us to consider how we pay attention to God's signs in our lives. The question is not just about seeing or hearing, but taking to heart — allowing our minds and feelings to be touched and transformed by what God does or says. It is an invitation to spiritual vigilance and conscious obedience.

sens: The fabric or clothing that covers the body
The outward appearance, the attire or dress of a person
That which envelops something in a way that covers or characterizes it
H7897.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a garment in the first sense: an article of clothing that covers the body. In Proverbs 7:10, the seducing woman is described as having "the attire of a harlot" — it is the whole of what dresses her, her outfit, the way she presents herself clothed.
2. In a broader sense, it means the outward appearance, that which is first seen: the attire, the dress, that which characterizes a person's presentation in the eyes of others.
3. Finally, it can describe that which envelops something in a way that identifies or reveals it. In Psalms 73:6, pride and violence are like garments that envelop the wicked: these are no longer literal clothes, but what characterizes them in the eyes of all, what morally and spiritually dresses them.
H7897.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means to cover or to clothe. The basic image is that of something that covers: just as a garment covers the body, this term can describe what surrounds, characterizes, or identifies someone or something. It is a concrete word whose meaning naturally extends to the idea of presentation and character.
H7897.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Bible in Hebrew. In Psalms 73:6, the psalmist sees pride and violence as garments that envelop the prosperous wicked — the image is that of an adornment that distinguishes and identifies them. In Proverbs 7:10, the seducing woman approaches the young man "having the attire of a harlot" — here the word designates the outfit, the appearance that reveals or displays her role. The meaning shifts from physical clothing to what is seen and speaks of a person: their attire, their appearance, what characterizes them in the eyes of others.
H7897.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on what "clothes" us in the eyes of others: not just our garments, but our reputation, our visible traits, what characterizes us. In Psalms 73:6, it warns us that pride and violence mark the wicked as visibly as a garment. In Proverbs 7:10, it reminds us that appearance can seduce and deceive. These passages urge us to scrutinize what truly dresses us: our invisible values rather than our deceptive appearance.

sens: Wild thorny shrub that grows in uncultivated land
Dense and impenetrable vegetation that invades abandoned lands
Image of sterility and divine destruction
Symbol of judgment and consumption by fire
H7898.detail:
1. The thorn is a brambly shrub, covered in thorns, that grows naturally in Mediterranean regions. In Isaiah 5:6, the Lord abandons His vineyard and it becomes covered with thorns, showing how fertile lands return to a wild and unproductive state when God withdraws His blessing.
2. Thorns characterize devastated and unusable lands. Isaiah 7:23-25 describes how valuable vineyards will be overrun by thorns and thistles, and that people will no longer dare to enter them for fear of this hostile vegetation. It is the image of a land rendered sterile and dangerous.
3. In the prophecies of Isaiah, the thorn represents divine judgment: it invades the lands when God withdraws His support and protection. In Isaiah 9:17 and 10:17, the thorn is consumed by fire, a symbol of the destruction and punishment that God sends against evil and wickedness.
H7898.origine: The Hebrew word שַׁיִת (shaïth) designates thorny plants that cover abandoned lands or lands struck by judgment. It belongs to the family of terms describing wild and hostile vegetation. In biblical Hebrew, this word stands in opposition to the cultivated vine and the harvest of tilled land: it embodies the return of territory to an uncultivated and unproductive state.
H7898.emploi: This word appears seven times in the book of Isaiah, always in the plural "thorns." Isaiah uses it in his oracles of judgment against Judah and Israel: prosperous and well-kept vineyards become fields of thorns when the Lord withdraws His favor (Isaiah 5:6; 7:23-25). The context is consistently one of desolation and abandonment: thorns drive away the inhabitants and render the lands unusable. In Isaiah 9:17 and 10:17, the thorn is burned by fire, which intensifies the image of divine judgment transformed into active and purifying destruction.
H7898.portee: The thorn teaches the reader that God's abandonment of a people or land produces visible and lasting desolation. It concretely shows that divine judgment is not invisible: it manifests through the ruin of human works and the sterility that overtakes the land. It is a call to repentance: those who listen to the word of Isaiah understand that returning to God is urgent, otherwise their cities and lands will become fields of thorns.

sens: Small sharp point that grows on a plant
That which wounds or persistently irritates
That which remains as an obstacle or enemy in the land one inhabits
H7899.detail: 1. The thorn is a small, sharp, and hard stem that naturally grows on certain plants: it pricks anyone who touches or brushes against it. 2. Figuratively, a thorn refers to something that constantly wounds or irritates — a constant annoyance, a source of pain or moral discomfort. 3. In the passage from Numbers 33:55, the inhabitants of the land that the Israelites do not drive out are described as thorns: they will remain as enemies that will prick relentlessly, permanent obstacles to peace and tranquility.
H7899.origine: The Hebrew word sekh literally means a thorn or sharp point. It belongs to the family of words that describe natural obstacles and irritants. The basic image is that of the thorny plant, which wounds the touch: hence comes the figurative meaning of persistent obstacle or enemy.
H7899.emploi: This word appears only once in Numbers 33:55, in the context of entering Canaan. Moses warns the Israelites: if they do not completely drive out the inhabitants of the land, they will become for them like thorns in their eyes and pricks in their sides — a very concrete image of what constantly wounds and irritates. It is a warning about the consequences of incomplete obedience to God's will.
H7899.portee: This passage teaches that obedience to God's plan must be complete: partially tolerating what He commands to be entirely eliminated creates lasting wounds. The thorn symbolizes how partial disobedience settles in as a permanent pain in the believer's life.
